Chapter 4 Energy principles and virtual work

4.6 Minimum total potential energy

In section 4.5 we wrote the equilibrium of a body as one single equation, the principle of virtual displacements. In the derivation we used no relation between stress and strain, so it holds for every material. In section 3.6, however, we met materials that store the work needed for a deformation and return all of it on unloading. What does the principle of virtual displacements say for a body made of such a material, when the material is also linearly elastic and stable and the loads do not change with the deformation (assumptions 2 to 4 below)? It says something that fits into one sentence: among all shapes that the supports allow, the body comes to rest in the one for which a certain number, the sum of the stored energy and the potential energy of the loads, is smallest. So we can also find the equilibrium by looking for the shape at which this sum is smallest.

From history

In 1740 Pierre Louis Moreau de Maupertuis, as he is credited, wrote that at an equilibrium to which a body returns after a small displacement the potential energy has its smallest value (EP, p. 3). Euler developed this thought on the elastica (elastika), the curve into which a thin bar bends. He showed that the equations follow from it that tell how a thin bar bends and at what compressive force it suddenly bends sideways (EP, p. 3). The expression for the bending energy was passed on to him by Daniel Bernoulli: the whole force that is in a curved elastic strip can be written with one formula, which he called the potential force, and for the true curve it must be a minimum (TIMO, PDF p. 40). For a strip that is straight in its natural position this is the integral \(\int \frac{1}{R^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\) over the arc length \(s\) measured along the curve, where \(R\) is the radius of the circle that fits the curve best at the given point. The integral is the number that the sums over short arcs, the length of each arc times \(1/R^2\) on it, approach as the arcs get ever shorter. Up to a constant factor this is the bending energy (TIMO, PDF p. 35 and 227). The first systematic treatment of the elastica was brought by Euler's book Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas of 1744 (TIMO, PDF p. 37).

The goal of the section is to state the claim about the smallest sum of the stored energy and the potential energy of the loads precisely, to prove it from the principle of virtual displacements for an arbitrary body, and to show what it is good for. It is good for three things. First, it gives a new way of computing displacements. Instead of writing the equilibrium for every part of a structure separately, we look for where one single function has its smallest value. For the bracket of two bars from section 4.1 this will be a function of two numbers, the horizontal and the vertical displacement of the joint, and the point where it is smallest will give the displacement of the joint without knowing the bar forces first. Second, it gives approximate solutions. When we cannot compute the true displacement field, we try a family of simple fields and choose the one with the smallest energy. The computation with trial fields and the finite element method, which we will meet in chapters 6 and 7, rest on this idea. Third, it tells how force is related to energy. The force on a structure is the derivative of the strain energy with respect to the displacement of the point it acts on. This relation bears Castigliano's name.

The physical model is the same as in section 4.5, with additions about the material and the loads. Let us list all assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. The body is at rest, the strains are small, and we compute all quantities on the shape of the body before loading, the strain with the small strain tensor (definition 1.121). This is how the principle of virtual displacements is written, and all proofs of the section stand on it.
  2. The material is ideal elastic (definition 3.58) and linear elastic. So the stress components are linear functions of the strain components, and the material stiffness matrix is symmetric (theorem 3.62). The strain energy density is therefore half the sum of the products of stresses and strains, \(w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (theorem 3.62, item 2). We use this when we express the energy of a body in equilibrium by the work of the loads, and in the proof of the principle. The assumption holds below the yield stress, for the steel of our examples up to 220 MPa. Above it part of the work is not returned on unloading, when the steel is stretched to the strain 0,002 as much as 61 % (section 4.1.2).
  3. The strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero. This is the assumption about a stable material from section 3.6, which for an isotropic material is equivalent to a positive bulk modulus and a positive shear modulus (theorem 3.64). We use it in the proof that the energy of the true field is smallest.
  4. The loads do not change with the deformation, neither in size nor in direction. Weight is such a load. What this means and why it is needed we say in subsection 4.6.3, where we use the assumption.
  5. Supports prescribe the displacements on a part of the surface. In the first theorem of the section we assume that these displacements are zero, as for a face that is glued or welded to an immovable wall.
  6. The displacement fields are continuously differentiable (definition 1.91), and the stresses of the true field have continuous partial derivatives, as the principle of virtual displacements requires. Where this fails, at a point force and at the interface of two materials, we saw in section 4.5.7.

The route is this. First, on a vertical bar with a load, where everything depends on one number, we show what potential energy is and why it is smallest in equilibrium. Then we derive from the principle of virtual displacements a theorem which says that the energy a body stores in equilibrium is half the work the loads would do if they were at full value all the time. The precise definition of the number we compare and the proof of the principle follow. We test the principle on the bracket of two bars, show how it is related to the principle of virtual displacements, and derive from it that a force is the derivative of the energy with respect to a displacement. At the end we test on the hanging bar what the energy of simple trial fields gives, fields that are not the true field.

4.6.1 A bar with a load

Let us start with the simplest body we know. We stand the steel bar from section 4.1 upright, with length \(L = 10\) m and a round cross section of diameter 10 mm and area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\). Its upper end is fixed to the ceiling so that it does not move. On its lower end we hang a load that weighs \(F = 10\) kN (figure 4.258). We neglect the weight of the bar, 60,10 N, because it is only 0,6 % of the weight of the load. It would increase the elongation by only 0,3 %, since every cross section carries only the weight of the part of the bar below it, on average half the weight (section 4.1). We may not neglect it for a bar whose weight is comparable to the weight of the load. The stress in the bar is then \(F/A = 127{,}3\) MPa, below the yield stress 220 MPa, so the force with which the bar pulls the load up is proportional to the elongation \(e\). This force is \(k\,e\), where \(k = EA/L = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, as in section 4.1, and \(E = 196\) GPa is Young's modulus of steel. The upper end is at rest, so the elongation \(e\) is also the downward displacement of the lower end, measured from the grey dashed line, the position of the lower end of the unstretched bar. The bar acts as a spring whose state is described by one single number, \(e\).

Where does the load come to rest? The load is in equilibrium when the bar pulls it up with a force as large as the weight pulls it down, \(k\,e = F\), so at the elongation

\[\Delta L = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{10\,000\ \text{N}}{1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m}} = 6{,}496\ \text{mm} .\]

We got there with forces. Now let us answer the same question with energy. Imagine that we hold the lower end with the load by hand at some elongation \(e\), not necessarily \(\Delta L\) (figure 4.258). The bar pulls the load up with the force \(k\,e\), the weight pulls it down with the force \(F\), and the hand must add the difference \(F - k\,e\) upward. At \(e = 0\) the hand carries the whole load, at \(e = \Delta L/2\) half of it, since \(k\,\Delta L/2 = F/2\), and at \(e = \Delta L\) nothing. All these states are possible, since in all of them the bar is fixed to the ceiling, but without the hand only the last one is in equilibrium. In each state the bar is stretched evenly, because only the two forces at its ends act on it. To each state we assign two energies.

The first is the strain energy of the bar. In section 4.1 we showed that the force that stretches the bar slowly to the elongation \(\Delta L\) does the work \(\tfrac12 k\,\Delta L^2\), and that the bar stores it as strain energy (theorem 4.3). The same statement holds for every final elongation, so at the elongation \(e\) the strain energy of the bar is \(U(e) = \tfrac12 k\,e^2\).

The second is the energy of the load. When the load is lowered by \(e\), the weight does the work \(F\,e\) on it, because it is a constant force pointing along the path, and its work is the product of force and path (definition 4.1). The load could pass this work on, for example by lifting another body over a pulley. When we lift the load back, however, we have to put the same work in ourselves. So the load holds a store of work that lowering uses up and lifting restores. This store is called the potential energy (potencialna energija) of the load. Only its change matters, so we choose it to be zero at \(e = 0\). At the elongation \(e\) the load is lower by \(e\), the weight has done the work \(F\,e\), and the potential energy of the load is \(-F\,e\). This is the school rule that the potential energy of a body equals its weight times its height, except that here the height is measured from the starting position and is therefore negative. EP uses the same example, a spring with a weight, to show that the work of the constant force of the load is not equal to the work of the internal force of the spring (EP §3.1.2, pp. 99-100).

The sum of the two energies is

\[\Pi(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2 - F\,e . \tag{4.53}\]

The table shows it for five states. The energies are in joules, computed with \(k\) and \(F\) above. At \(2\Delta L\) the stress would be \(2 \cdot 127{,}3\ \text{MPa} = 254{,}6\) MPa, above the yield stress 220 MPa, since the force of the bar reaches \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} A = 17{,}28\) kN already at the elongation \(1{,}728\,\Delta L = 11{,}22\) mm (section 4.1). So the last row describes a bar that would stay linearly elastic. Our steel bar would deform permanently before \(2\Delta L\).

elongation \(e\) \(U(e) = \tfrac12 k\,e^2\) \(-F\,e\) \(\Pi(e)\)
\(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)
\(\Delta L/2 = 3{,}248\) mm \(8{,}120\) \(-32{,}48\) \(-24{,}36\)
\(\Delta L = 6{,}496\) mm \(32{,}48\) \(-64{,}96\) \(-32{,}48\)
\(3\Delta L/2 = 9{,}744\) mm \(73{,}08\) \(-97{,}44\) \(-24{,}36\)
\(2\Delta L = 12{,}99\) mm \(129{,}9\) \(-129{,}9\) \(0\)

Figure 4.259 shows the strain energy \(U\) as the blue parabola, the potential energy of the load \(-F\,e\) as the grey line and their sum \(\Pi\) as the blackwhite parabola, all against the elongation \(e\). The sum is lowest at \(\Delta L\), where \(\Pi = -32{,}48\) J, \(U = 32{,}48\) J and \(-F\,\Delta L = -64{,}96\) J, and at \(2\,\Delta L\) it is zero again. The table shows three patterns. The sum \(\Pi\) is smallest at \(e = \Delta L\), exactly at equilibrium. The values at elongations equally far to the left and to the right of \(\Delta L\) are equal, at \(\Delta L/2\) and at \(3\Delta L/2\) it is \(-24{,}36\) J. At \(2\Delta L\) the sum is zero again, as at the start. Where does all this come from? Let us rewrite the sum so that it shows how it depends on the distance from \(\Delta L\).

  1. We expand the square of the difference as the product \((e - \Delta L)(e - \Delta L)\): we multiply every term of the first bracket by every term of the second and get \(e^2 - 2\,e\,\Delta L + \Delta L^2\). Therefore
    \[\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2 = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2 - k\,\Delta L\,e + \tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 .\]
  2. The equilibrium elongation satisfies \(k\,\Delta L = F\). So the middle term is \(k\,\Delta L\,e = F\,e\), and the last one is \(\tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 = \tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\).
  3. From step 1 we express \(\tfrac12\,k\,e^2 - F\,e\) and insert step 2:
    \[\Pi(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2 - \tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L . \tag{4.54}\]

The first term is half the positive number \(k\) times a square, so it is never negative and is zero only at \(e = \Delta L\). The second term does not depend on \(e\). The sum is therefore smallest at \(e = \Delta L\), where \(\Pi(\Delta L) = -\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L = -32{,}48\) J. The first term depends only on the distance \(|e - \Delta L|\), so the values at \(\Delta L/2\) and \(3\Delta L/2\) are equal. There the distance is \(\Delta L/2\) and the first term is \(\tfrac12\,k\,(\Delta L/2)^2 = 8{,}12\) J, as much as \(U\) at \(\Delta L/2\) in the table, and indeed \(-32{,}48 + 8{,}12 = -24{,}36\) J. At \(e = 2\Delta L\) the distance is again \(\Delta L\), the first term is \(\tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 = \tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L = 32{,}48\) J and cancels the second to zero. But the first term is one more thing: the strain energy the bar would have if it were stretched by the difference \(e - \Delta L\). By how much the energy of a state exceeds the energy of equilibrium is thus told by the strain energy of the difference of the two elongations. This will be the core of the proof for every body.

Why is the smallest value exactly at equilibrium? By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82) the derivative of \(\Pi\) with respect to \(e\) is \(k\,e - F\), the force with which the bar pulls the load up, minus the weight of the load. This is the negative of the force \(F - k\,e\) that the hand has to add. For \(e < \Delta L\) the derivative is negative. The weight overcomes the bar, and a load that the hand lets go starts to move down, toward smaller energy. For \(e > \Delta L\) the derivative is positive, the bar overcomes the weight, and the load starts to move up, again toward smaller energy. Without the hand the load is in equilibrium only where the derivative is zero, and that is at \(e = \Delta L\), where \(\Pi\) has its smallest value.

We can say the same with a picture everyone knows. The graph of the sum \(\Pi\) is a bowl and the load a marble on its wall: wherever we put it, it starts to roll down the wall from there, as the orange arrows show, and it rests only at the bottom. This view adds the direction without a calculation: we read from the picture where the released load moves, without comparing the two forces. It does not tell how far the load goes. The calculation of work below tells that.

And what does the smallest value itself, \(-\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\), mean? In equilibrium the load is lower by \(\Delta L\) than at the start, the weight has done the work \(F\,\Delta L = 64{,}96\) J, but the bar stores only \(\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L = 32{,}48\) J (figure 4.260). In the figure the force of the bar \(k\,e\) is the blackwhite line, the weight \(F\) the horizontal line, and on the axis of the elongation the value \(\Delta L\) is the equilibrium. The blue triangle under the line is the energy the bar stores. Where did the other half go? It depends on how we lower the load. If we lower it slowly by hand, the hand pushes up with the force \(F - k\,e\) all the time, in the figure the height of the grey triangle at the elongation \(e\), while the load moves down. Slowly means that the kinetic energy of the load is negligible: at a speed of 1 mm/s the load of mass \(F/g = 1019\) kg has the kinetic energy \(0{,}51\) mJ, only \(0{,}0016\) % of \(32{,}48\) J. The force of the hand and the displacement point in opposite directions, so the hand does negative work. The function \(F\,e - \tfrac12\,k\,e^2\) has the derivative \(F - k\,e\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55 the work of the hand is

\[-\int_0^{\Delta L} (F - k\,e)\,\mathrm{d}e = -\Big(F\,\Delta L - \tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2\Big) = -\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L ,\]

where we used \(k\,\Delta L = F\). So the hand receives exactly the other half, the grey triangle in figure 4.260. If instead we let the load go suddenly at \(e = 0\), the hand receives nothing, and the difference goes into motion. In section 4.1 we saw that the load then slides past \(\Delta L\) and, without damping, would stop only at \(2\,\Delta L\) and oscillate about \(\Delta L\) if the bar stayed linearly elastic (CK §5.1, PDF p. 137). Our steel bar, however, reaches the yield stress already at \(11{,}22\) mm and would deform permanently, so the reckoning up to \(2\,\Delta L\) below holds for a bar that stays elastic. Why exactly there? Between \(\Delta L\) and \(2\,\Delta L\) the bar pulls harder than the weight, and the excess \(k\,e - F\) brakes the motion. The work it takes out of the motion is the orange triangle above the weight, with base \(\Delta L\) and height \(2F - F = F\), so \(\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L = 32{,}48\) J. That is exactly as much as the grey triangle gave to the motion. At \(2\,\Delta L\) the energy \(\Pi\) is zero again, as at the start, so the zero in the last row of the table is no coincidence: there the strain energy of the bar uses up exactly the work of the weight.

The bar with a load has shown the idea that we now carry over to a body. We compare all states that the supports allow, not only the equilibrium one. To each state we assign the sum of the strain energy and the potential energy of the loads. The equilibrium state has the smallest sum, and the difference to every other state is the strain energy of the difference of the displacements, \(\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2\). We also saw that the strain energy in equilibrium is half the work the weight would do over the whole displacement. Let us start with this observation.

4.6.2 Clapeyron's theorem

Let us return to the body from section 4.5 (figure 4.226). Before loading the body occupies the set of points \(V\) with surface \(S\). On the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface there are supports, here a wall, that prescribe the displacements. On the rest of the surface, \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) with which the surroundings act on the body is prescribed. On the free parts of the surface \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). A body force with density \(\vek b\) (definition 2.28) acts on the material, for example the weight. The stresses in the body are continuously differentiable, symmetric, satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.38) in the interior and Cauchy's formula \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal. The principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.82) then says that

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\delta\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\]

for every kinematically admissible virtual displacement \(\delta\vek u\), that is for every continuously differentiable field that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (definition 4.79). Here \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the components of its virtual strain, and the indices \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

In section 4.1 we got the strain energy of a bar by multiplying the energy density \(w\) by the area of the cross section and integrating along the length. In a body that is not a bar the energy density can change in all three directions. Figure 4.261 shows such a body on the left. The left face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is held by a wall, and the prescribed force \(\bar{\vek t}\) presses on the right part of the top face. Grey dashed is the body before loading, orange the body after it, with the displacements strongly exaggerated. A small piece of the body with volume \(\Delta V\) at the point \(P\) stores approximately \(w(P)\,\Delta V\). The energy of the body is the sum of the energies of its pieces, and when we shrink the pieces, the sum becomes an integral over the body (section 4.2).

Definition 4.85 Strain energy of a body (deformacijska energija telesa)

Let a body occupy the set of points \(V\), a set with volume (definition 4.27), and let the material be ideal elastic and the strain small at every point, with a strain energy density \(w\) (definition 3.59) that is a continuous function of the point on \(V\). The strain energy (deformacijska energija) of the body is the number we get by adding up the energies of all the pieces

\[U = \int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

Source: EP (3.2.8) (p. 106) and (4.3.4) (p. 180), SADD §6.1 (PDF pp. 128-131), CM (7.6.11) (PDF p. 345).

Let us test the definition on the bar of figure 4.6, pulled at its end with the force 10 kN. The energy density is the same in the whole bar, \(w = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon = 4{,}136 \cdot 10^4\ \text{J/m}^3\) (section 4.1), the volume of the bar is \(A L = 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3\), and by the rule for the integral of a constant function over the round bar (section 4.2.8) \(U = 4{,}136 \cdot 10^4\ \text{J/m}^3 \cdot 7{,}854 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3 = 32{,}48\) J, as it should be: this is the area of the triangle under the line of the force, the work of the force at the end.

For the bar with a load the strain energy in equilibrium was half the product of the weight of the load and the displacement, \(\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\). Does this hold for every body? It does for every linear elastic body with fixed supports at small strains, and the proof is short, because the principle of virtual displacements does all the work.

From history

B. P. E. Clapeyron and Lamé served as French engineers in Russia. For the reconstruction of Saint Isaac's cathedral in Saint Petersburg they studied the stability of arches (TIMO, PDF p. 123). In 1831 Clapeyron returned to France, where he worked mostly on the building of railways and on the use of thermodynamics in the design of locomotives (TIMO, PDF p. 126). He stated the theorem we will prove long before Lamé's book of 1852 appeared. It says that the sum of the products of the external forces and the corresponding displacements equals twice the strain energy, and this was the first general expression for the strain energy of a deformed isotropic body (TIMO, PDF p. 126). Lamé described it in his book on elasticity and attributed it to Clapeyron (TIMO, PDF p. 126, 227). Clapeyron came to the theorem through springs. Studying various kinds of springs he concluded that the energy an elastic body stores and returns on unloading is proportional to its volume, so he asked how to express this work (TP2A, PDF p. 446). The sources do not agree on the credit. TIMO says that Clapeyron stated the theorem, and EP says that Lamé was the first to prove the work equation (delovna enačba) for deformable bodies, in 1852, that is, the equation that makes the work of the external forces equal to the energy of the body, and named it after Clapeyron (EP, p. 3). TP2A (PDF p. 446-447) adds that Lamé and Clapeyron had already written the expression for twice the work of an elastic body, in terms of the principal stresses, in a joint memoir of 1833, and holds that it is entirely Clapeyron's, because Lamé in 1852 calls it Clapeyron's theorem and Clapeyron in a paper of 1858 speaks of it as his own.

Where the half comes from is shown by the right half of figure 4.261 even before the proof. Look at one piece and the force on it. While the loads grow slowly, the point \(P\) travels along a straight segment to its final position. On the horizontal axis of the graph is the distance \(s\) it has already travelled, on the vertical axis the projection of the force on the direction of motion. The force grows together with the displacement, along the blackwhite line from zero to its full value: when the point is halfway, the force is half. The work of such a force is the blue triangle, \(\tfrac12\,\vek b\cdot\vek u\,\Delta V\). If the force were at full value all the time, on the grey horizontal line, the work would be the whole rectangle, \(\vek b\cdot\vek u\,\Delta V\), twice as much: the blue triangle would be joined by the equally large grey triangle above the line. The theorem that follows adds up the rectangles of all pieces and patches and says that the sum is twice the energy of the body.

Theorem 4.86 Clapeyron's theorem (Clapeyronov izrek)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.82 on the principle of virtual displacements, made of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material. Let \(\vek u\) be the displacement field of the body in equilibrium, continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, equal to zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and with small strains at every point of the body, and let its stresses satisfy assumptions 1 to 4 of theorem 4.82. Then the strain energy of the body is half the work that the body force and the prescribed force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) would do on the displacements \(\vek u\) if they were at full value all the time:

\[2\,U = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.55}\]
Proof

We have to show that the two sides of the principle of virtual displacements become the two sides of equation (4.55) when we take the true displacement field as the virtual displacement.

  1. The field \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body with its surface, and it is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), because the wall does not move, so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.79). In the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.82) we may therefore take \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\).
  2. The virtual strain of the field \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\) is the small strain tensor of the body in equilibrium, because both are computed from the same partial derivatives, \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The left side of the principle is therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  3. By the assumption of the theorem the strain is small at every point, and the material is ideal elastic and linear elastic, so by theorem 3.62 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, item 2, at every point \(\sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\,w\). For the bar, where there is only one stress, this is figure 4.6 with both axes divided by the dimensions of the bar: the energy density is the triangle under the line, \(w = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\), and the product \(\sigma\,\varepsilon\) is the rectangle, twice as much.
  4. The function \(w\) is continuous, because the stresses are continuous by assumption 1 of theorem 4.82 and the strains are too, as derivatives of the continuously differentiable field \(\vek u\), so \(U\) is defined (definition 4.85). By the linearity of the integral over a body (section 4.2) the integral of the function \(2\,w\) is twice the integral of \(w\). The left side is therefore \(2\int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\mathrm{d}V = 2\,U\) (definition 4.85).
  5. The right side of the principle at \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\) is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\), the sum of the rectangles of all pieces and patches. The two sides are equal, which is (4.55).

Source: EP Theorem 4.6.1, (4.6.10) (pp. 220-221), SADD (6.4.1) (PDF p. 135), CM §7.4 (PDF pp. 314-321). EP and SADD prove the theorem directly with the divergence theorem. We got it from the principle of virtual displacements, which had already taken that step.

In the proof we took the true displacement as the virtual one. In section 4.4 a virtual displacement meant an imagined displacement with the forces unchanged, while the true displacement is the one the forces really cause. May we do this? We may, because as a mathematical statement the principle of virtual displacements asks only two things of the field \(\delta\vek u\): that it is continuously differentiable and that it is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The true field meets both, the first by the assumption of theorem 4.86 on the field \(\vek u\), the second because the supports do not move. The principle does not ask the displacement to be small, because both sides are multiplied by the same number when the field is multiplied by a number (section 4.5).

The right side of equation (4.55) is thus the work the loads would do if they were as large during the whole motion as at its end, like the load on the bar. For the bar with a load this was the rectangle with sides \(F\) and \(\Delta L\), \(F\,\Delta L = 64{,}96\) J, and the bar stored the blue half, \(32{,}48\) J. In slow loading, however, the loads grow from zero, and each does only the triangle, half the product of final force and final displacement. It follows from Clapeyron's theorem that for every linear elastic body with fixed supports this work is stored completely. In section 4.1 we checked this for the bar and for the hanging bar and promised a proof for every body. Let us write it down.

Corollary 4.87 Work of the loads and strain energy (delo obremenitev in deformacijska energija)

Let the body, its material and the displacement field \(\vek u\) be as in theorem 4.86. Let the loads grow slowly from zero to their final values, all in the same proportion: at a number \(\lambda\) between \(0\) and \(1\) the body force is \(\lambda\,\vek b\) and the prescribed force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is \(\lambda\,\bar{\vek t}\). Let the body take the state with displacements \(\lambda\,\vek u\) at every \(\lambda\). Let the work of the loads on the body be the sum of the works on the pieces and on the patches of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the same number for every cutting, and let the work on a piece with volume \(\Delta V\) lie between the least and the greatest value of the expression \(\tfrac12\,\vek b\cdot\vek u\,\Delta V\) over its points, and likewise for a patch with area \(\Delta A\) and the expression \(\tfrac12\,\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\Delta A\). Then the work of the loads in this loading equals the strain energy of the body in the final state,

\[W_{\mathrm{zun}} = \tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A = U .\]
Proof

We have to show that every bit of the load does half the product of final force and final displacement, then write the sum as an integral and use Clapeyron's theorem.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of the body with \(\vek u(P) \ne \vek 0\). At the number \(\lambda\) its displacement is \(\lambda\,\vek u(P)\), so the point moves along a straight segment from its position before loading to its position after loading, in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek d = \vek u(P)/|\vek u(P)|\). When it has travelled the distance \(s\), \(\lambda = s/|\vek u(P)|\).
  2. If we think of the whole force of a piece with volume \(\Delta V\) as applied at the point \(P\), at \(\lambda\) it is \(\lambda\,\vek b(P)\,\Delta V\). Its projection onto the direction of motion is \((s/|\vek u(P)|)\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek d\,\Delta V\), a point on the blackwhite line of the graph. The work is the area of the triangle under the line, which we compute with an integral. The function \(s^2/2\) has the derivative \(s\), so by item 2 of definition 4.1 and the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55 the work of this force is
    \[\int_0^{|\vek u(P)|} \frac{s}{|\vek u(P)|}\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek d\,\Delta V\,\mathrm{d}s = \tfrac12\,|\vek u(P)|\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek d\,\Delta V = \tfrac12\,\vek b(P)\cdot\vek u(P)\,\Delta V .\]
    At \(\vek u(P) = \vek 0\) the point does not move, the work is zero, and the formula gives the same.
  1. Definition 4.1 speaks of a force on one point, but a piece has points with different displacements. So in the corollary we assumed what step 2 shows for one point: the work of the load on a piece lies between the least and the greatest value of the expression \(\tfrac12\,\vek b\cdot\vek u\,\Delta V\) over the points of the piece. We assumed the same for a patch with area \(\Delta A\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and the expression \(\tfrac12\,\bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\Delta A\). Figure 4.262 shows this on the hanging bar that we will test below, with the axis \(x\) pointing down. The width of the blackwhite curve at the depth \(x\) is the work per unit length that the weight does in slow loading, \(\tfrac12\,q\,u(x)\), \(58{,}65\) µJ/m at the bottom. We cut the bar into pieces of length \(h\). On one piece the displacement is least at the top and greatest at the bottom, so by the assumption the work on it lies between the area of the blue column, as wide as the curve at the top of the piece, and the area of the column with the orange excess, as wide as the curve at the bottom. The assumption is reasonable because within a small piece the displacement changes little from point to point. At the bottom of the hanging bar below (figure 4.263) the displacement of the cross section at the depth \(9\) m, \(19{,}32\) µm, differs from the displacement of the lower end, \(19{,}52\) µm, by \(1\) %, and over the last \(10\) cm only by \(0{,}01\) %. So the least and the greatest value on a piece come together as the pieces shrink, and step 4 shows that the assumption leaves no error at all in the final result. It would fail where the displacement is not continuous, for example at a crack, which the assumptions of the theorem exclude. The forces of the supports on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) do no work, because \(\vek u = \vek 0\) there.
  2. Let \(\eta > 0\). We cut the body with a grid into cells (section 4.2.10). By the assumption of the corollary the work of the body is the sum of the works of the cells and does not depend on the grid. The cells in \(V\) are the pieces. The function \(\tfrac12\,\vek b\cdot\vek u\) is continuous, so on every cell it reaches its least and greatest value. By step 3 the work of the cells in \(V\) lies between the sum of the least values and the sum of the greatest values, multiplied by the volumes of the cells. For five pieces of the hanging bar the blue columns add up to \(328{,}46\) µJ, with the orange excesses to \(445{,}77\) µJ, and the area under the curve, \(391{,}03\) µJ, lies between them. The difference of the sums is the sum of the excesses. The curve only grows downward, so the excesses, moved to the same height, meet without overlapping and fill a strip of height \(h\) and width \(58{,}65\) µJ/m, \(58{,}65\ \text{µJ/m} \cdot 2\ \text{m} = 117{,}31\) µJ. For twenty pieces the strip is four times lower, \(29{,}33\) µJ, and both sums are closer to the integral. Both are sums of definition 4.30 with a special choice of points, so for a fine enough grid they are within \(\eta\) of the integral \(\tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V\) (theorem 4.31). The function is bounded on the closed and bounded set \(V\) (theorem 1.79): there is a number \(M > 0\) with \(|\tfrac12\,\vek b\cdot\vek u| \le M\) everywhere. By lemma 4.29, item 3, the boundary cells have total volume less than \(\eta/M\) for a fine enough grid, so by step 3 their work is less than \(\eta\) in absolute value. So the work of the body differs from the integral by less than \(2\,\eta\). Since \(\eta\) is arbitrary and the work does not depend on the grid, the difference is less than every positive number, so it is zero, and the work of the body equals the integral. Likewise the work of the patches on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) equals the surface integral (definition 4.11, item 3, on every face theorem 4.31 in the plane). The work of the loads is therefore \(\tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \tfrac12 \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  3. By Clapeyron's theorem 4.86 this is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 2\,U = U\).

Source: CM (7.4.4) (PDF p. 315), SADD §6.1 (PDF p. 128), EP p. 100. The work of body and surface forces as \(\int \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V + \int \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\): EP (3.1.7) (p. 99), LOVE §120 (PDF p. 192, where the strain energy is half of this work). Step 3 is ours: the sources write the work of distributed loads directly as integrals and do not derive it from the work of forces on points. The step-by-step proof is not from the sources.

The corollary assumes that the body takes the state \(\lambda\,\vek u\) at every \(\lambda\). Why is this reasonable? In figure 4.261 this is the dot on the displacement segment, which at half the force is halfway along the path. Under the loads \(\lambda\,\vek b\) and \(\lambda\,\bar{\vek t}\) the field \(\lambda\,\vek u\) meets all the requirements of equilibrium. The stresses are linear functions of the strains, so the stresses of the field \(\lambda\,\vek u\) are \(\lambda\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The equilibrium equations and Cauchy's formula are linear, so \(\lambda\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) satisfy them with the loads \(\lambda\,\vek b\) and \(\lambda\,\bar{\vek t}\) when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) satisfy them with \(\vek b\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\). That the body takes exactly this state and not some other follows from item 2 of theorem 4.91, proved below, when the energy density is positive at every small strain that is not zero and the supports prevent every displacement without strain. By item 1 of the theorem each of two equilibrium fields has a \(\Pi\) less than or equal to that of the other, so the same one, and by item 2 their difference therefore has no strain and the supports make it zero. We used the same argument for the hanging bar in section 4.1.

The corollary has two more assumptions, and for each let us say what it costs. The first is the word slowly. The body is in equilibrium at every \(\lambda\), so no work goes into motion. If we let go of the load on the bar suddenly, the weight acts at full value from the start and on the way to the equilibrium position does the whole rectangle, \(64{,}96\) J. The bar stores the blue triangle, \(32{,}48\) J, while the grey triangle becomes kinetic energy, and the load swings up and down. The work of the loads is then not equal to \(U\). The second is that all loads grow in the same proportion. We need it so that the points travel along straight segments and the force on every piece is proportional to the distance travelled. If we apply one load first and then another, the work is divided between them differently, but for a linear elastic body their sum is the same, which we show on the truss in section 4.8.3.

Let us test the theorem on the hanging bar (figure 4.263, left). A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m and cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) hangs under its own weight, the axis \(x\) points down from the top cross section. We describe it with the bar model from section 4.1, in which every cross section moves only down, by \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), while the top cross section does not move. The lower end moves by \(u(L) = a\,L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm, strongly exaggerated in the figure. The weight per unit length is \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m. In section 4.1 we computed \(U = 391{,}03\) µJ. The work of the weight over the whole displacement, if the weight were at full value all the time, is

\[\int_0^L q\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \rho g A\,a \int_0^L (2Lx - x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac23\,\rho g A\,a\,L^3 = 782{,}06\ \text{µJ} ,\]

where we computed the integral by the fundamental theorem of calculus with the function \(Lx^2 - x^3/3\), whose derivative is \(2Lx - x^2\). This is exactly \(2\,U\), as Clapeyron's theorem says: the grey shape has twice the area of the blue one. For the hanging bar the same equality, \(\int_0^L N\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,u\,\mathrm{d}x\), already follows from section 4.4.8, but there we did not connect it with energy. There we checked the equality \(\int_0^L N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,\delta u\,\mathrm{d}x\) for the virtual displacements \(c\,x\) and \(c\,x^2/L\). Both sides are linear in \(\delta u\), and \(u = 2aL \cdot x + (-aL) \cdot x^2/L\) is the sum of the two displacements with \(c = 2aL\) and with \(c = -aL\), so the equality also holds at \(\delta u = u\). The bar model is not the body of the theorem, since it is described by one single function \(u(x)\). For it we get the theorem from the principle of virtual displacements for a bar (theorem 4.76), taking \(\delta u = u\) and the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\), with the same steps as above.

Figure 4.263 shows one more thing that the equality of two numbers does not: where the work is done and where the energy is stored. On the right is the work of the full weight per unit length, \(q\,u(x)\), drawn as the width of the grey shape at the depth \(x\), measured from the vertical line to the right. At the top it is zero, because the top cross section does not move, at the bottom it is greatest, \(q\,a\,L^2 = 117{,}31\) µJ/m, because the lower end moves the most. The area of the grey shape is \(782{,}06\) µJ. In the middle is the strain energy per unit length, the density \(w\) times the area of the cross section, \(A\,w = q\,a\,(L - x)^2\), again a width measured from the vertical line. At the top it is greatest, also \(117{,}31\) µJ/m, because the top cross section carries the whole weight, at the bottom it is zero, because the bottom cross section carries nothing. The area of the blue shape is \(U = 391{,}03\) µJ. Both shapes lie in equal rectangles with the area \(117{,}31\ \text{µJ/m} \cdot 10\ \text{m} = 1173{,}1\) µJ. The blue one fills a third of the rectangle and the grey one two thirds, because the sum of their widths at every depth is \(q\,a\,(L - x)^2 + q\,a\,(2Lx - x^2) = q\,a\,L^2\). So the weight does most of its work at the bottom, while the energy is stored at the top. Clapeyron's theorem does not claim that the work is stored where it is done. Only the sums over the whole body are equal, and this is why the theorem needs an integral over the body and the principle of virtual displacements, a computation at one point is not enough.

When does the theorem fail? First, when the supports prescribe displacements that are not zero, for example when we move one end of a bar by a chosen distance. Then the forces of the supports do work too, and the theorem holds if on the right we take, instead of the integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the integral of the force per unit area \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) times the displacement over the whole surface \(S\) (EP (4.6.10), p. 221). Our proof does not cover this case, because the true field is then not zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and is not a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. How far off we would be is shown by the bar of figure 4.6: if a grip moves its end by \(6{,}496\) mm instead of a prescribed force pulling it, the force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero everywhere, the right side of equation (4.55) is \(0\) J, and yet the bar stores \(U = 32{,}48\) J.

Second, for a material that is not linear elastic, for example rubber, the energy density is not half the sum of the products of stresses and strains (section 3.6), and step 3 of the proof fails. To get a feeling, take a bar and draw in figure 4.264 the stress against the strain. On the left is the line of a linear elastic material, and the triangle under it is the energy density \(w = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\), half the rectangle with sides \(\varepsilon\) and \(\sigma\). On the right is a material in which the stress grows with the square of the strain, \(\sigma = c\,\varepsilon^2\). The energy density is the area under this curve. The function \(c\,\varepsilon^3/3\) has the derivative \(c\,\varepsilon^2\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55 \(w = \tfrac13\,c\,\varepsilon^3 = \tfrac13\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\), a third of the rectangle, and the shape above the curve is two thirds. The left side of the principle at \(\delta\vek u = \vek u\) is the integral of the rectangles \(\sigma\,\varepsilon\), so the left side of the theorem would read \(3\,U\) instead of \(2\,U\). Third, for large deformations, where the principle of virtual displacements does not hold in this form (section 4.5). For the steel of our examples the strain up to the yield stress 220 MPa is at most \(220\ \text{MPa} / 196\ \text{GPa} = 0{,}0011\), so this case concerns rubber and similar materials, not steel in its elastic range.

4.6.3 Total potential energy

For the bar with a load we compared the states that the supports allow. For a body we need the same: displacement fields that agree with the prescribed displacements at the supports and are arbitrary elsewhere. They need not be true, and the body need not be in equilibrium in them. For the bar such a state was every elongation \(e\) at which the hand held the load (figure 4.258).

Definition 4.88 Kinematically admissible displacement field (kinematično dopustno polje pomikov)

Let a body occupy the set of points \(V\) before loading, and let the displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) be prescribed on the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of its surface. A displacement field \(\vek u\) is kinematically admissible (kinematično dopustno) if it is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface and equals the prescribed displacement at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\).

Source: EP (4.3.13) (p. 181), where the admissible fields satisfy \(\vek u = \hat{\vek u}\) on \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{u}}\), CM (PDF p. 346), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139).

The word kinematically says here too that only displacements are involved, not forces. The requirement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) means that the field respects the supports: the line of the field must pass through the prescribed point. Continuous differentiability makes sure that the field has a small strain tensor at every point and, where the strain is small, a strain energy density. The difference of two kinematically admissible fields is continuously differentiable and equals \(\bar{\vek u} - \bar{\vek u} = \vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.79). We will need this in the proof.

Let us look at which field the definition rejects (figure 4.265). A bar lies along the axis \(x\), and at \(x = 0\) the support has settled and has a prescribed displacement \(\bar u = 0{,}002\) mm. The field \(u = 0{,}002\ \text{mm} + \varepsilon x\), where \(\varepsilon\) is an arbitrary constant strain, is kinematically admissible: it is continuously differentiable and has the displacement \(0{,}002\) mm at \(x = 0\). The figure is drawn for \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\), that is \(0{,}001\) mm per metre. The field \(u = \varepsilon x\) is also continuously differentiable and has the same strain \(\varepsilon\), but at \(x = 0\) we have \(u = 0 \neq 0{,}002\) mm, so it is not kinematically admissible. It differs from the admissible one only by \(0{,}002\) mm, and yet it fails: the requirement \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) must be met exactly, not approximately, since otherwise the support would stay unmoved in the computation. The difference of two admissible fields, for example of \(0{,}002\ \text{mm} + 2\varepsilon x\) and \(0{,}002\ \text{mm} + \varepsilon x\), \(0{,}002\ \text{mm} + 2\varepsilon x - (0{,}002\ \text{mm} + \varepsilon x) = \varepsilon x\), is indeed zero at \(x = 0\), so it is a virtual displacement. At \(x = 3\) m this difference is \(0{,}003\) mm, exactly the height of the grey dashed line. The same field \(\varepsilon x\) is thus an admissible virtual displacement but not an admissible displacement field: a virtual displacement must not move the support, while a displacement field must move it by the prescribed settlement.

Now we still need the potential energy of the loads. For the load on the bar we got it from the work of the weight, \(-F\,e\). There we used that the weight is the same at every elongation, so its work was the product of a constant force and the path. The same holds for every load that does not change with the deformation, neither in size nor in direction. Such a load is called a dead load (obremenitev, neodvisna od deformacije), and weight is the most important example (figure 4.266, left). A constant force \(\vek F\) whose point of application moves by \(\vek u\), like the weight of the plate from the grey dot to the blackwhite one, does the work \(\vek F\cdot\vek u\) on the straight path (definition 4.1), and the potential energy of such a force is \(-\vek F\cdot\vek u\). For the body force and for the prescribed force on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) we add up the contributions of the pieces and patches and shrink them, as for the strain energy. The potential energy of the loads is therefore

\[-\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\]

(EP §3.3.1, p. 124).

Which loads are not like this? Figure 4.266 shows a plate fixed at the bottom that tilts by the angle \(\varphi\). On the left the weight acts on it. Before tilting and after it it points straight down and has the same size, only its point of application has moved. On the right water touches the plate. Water presses perpendicular to the surface it touches (section 2.6.6). Before tilting its force is horizontal, after it it is perpendicular to the tilted face, so it is turned by the same angle \(\varphi\). The direction of the load has changed with the deformation. Similarly the force of a rope fastened to a point of the body and to a fixed point in the surroundings changes when the point of the body moves sideways.

What does this cost? A force of size \(F\) turned by the angle \(\varphi\) has the component \(F\cos\varphi\) in the original direction and gains the transverse component \(F\sin\varphi\), the blue dashed segments in figure 4.266, where the angle is \(20^\circ\) for clarity. So the share \(\sin\varphi\) of the force appears across, and the force loses the share \(1 - \cos\varphi\) in the original direction. Figure 4.267 shows both in per cent of the force on the vertical axes, and the angle \(\varphi\) in radians on the horizontal ones. How large is \(\varphi\) at small deformations? A face turns because its fibres tilt, and the tilt of a fibre is given by the partial derivatives of the displacements (section 1.17.1). The small deformation assumption bounds them by \(m\) (section 1.17.3), so \(\varphi\) is at most about \(m\). The bound \(m\) is not the bound of the strains of steel, \(0{,}001\): a thin steel ruler turns by \(30^\circ\) at its end, although the strain of its surface is only \(0{,}00087\). So we take \(m = 0{,}01\), where the small strain tensor misses the strain of a fibre by at most \(4{,}5\) % of the bound \(m\) (the table in section 1.17.3). At \(\varphi = 0{,}01\) the transverse component is \(1\) % of the force, and the component in the original direction is smaller by \(0{,}005\) %. We read both shares on the left graph, which is the square at the origin of the right graph, magnified 20 times, since on the right graph we would not see them. For small deformations these changes are thus small, and we treat the load as independent of the deformation. At \(\varphi = 0{,}2\), that is \(11{,}5^\circ\), the transverse component is already \(20\) % of the force and the original one is smaller by \(2\) %. For large rotations such loads therefore have no potential energy of this form. EP defines the potential energy of the loads only for forces that are independent of the deformation (EP §3.3.1, p. 124).

Definition 4.89 Total potential energy (celotna potencialna energija)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.82 on the principle of virtual displacements, made of an ideal elastic material with strain energy density \(w\), with the displacement prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), a body force with density \(\vek b\) and a prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where \(\vek b\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\) are independent of the deformation. The total potential energy (celotna potencialna energija) of the body at a kinematically admissible displacement field \(\vek u\) with small strains, for which \(w\) is a continuous function of the point on \(V\), is the number, like the height of the blackwhite parabola at a chosen extension of the bar with the load,

\[\Pi(\vek u) = U(\vek u) - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad U(\vek u) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\mathrm{d}V , \tag{4.56}\]

where \(w\) at every point is computed from the components of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\) at that point.

Source: EP (3.3.1) (p. 124) and (4.3.7) (p. 180), CM (7.6.11)-(7.6.13) (PDF p. 345), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139), where \(\Pi = U_{\mathrm{T}} - W\).

What kind of object is \(\Pi\)? A function whose input is a whole displacement field and whose output is one number in joules. The function \(\Pi(e)\) of the bar with a load had one number as its input, because one number described the whole state. Here the input is a field that assigns a displacement to every point of the body. Books call such functions functionals (funkcionali) (CM, PDF p. 343). The first term is the strain energy of the body at the field \(\vek u\). The notation \(U(\vek u)\) says that the energy is computed from this field, which need not be the true one. The two conditions on \(\vek u\) in the definition make sure that this number exists: the density \(w\) is defined only at a small strain (definition 3.59), and the integral over the body exists when the function under it is continuous (theorem 4.31). The other two terms are the potential energy of the loads. For the bar with a load \(U(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2\) and the potential energy of the load is \(-F\,e\), so the definition gives \(\Pi(e)\) from equation (4.53), the blackwhite parabola in figure 4.259.

That the input really is a whole field is shown by figure 4.268 on the same bar, which we now regard as a body with a displacement field and not as a spring. On each of the three graphs the horizontal axis is the distance \(x\) of a cross-section from the ceiling, the vertical one its downward displacement \(u\) in millimetres. At the bottom is the true field \(u = \Delta L\,x/L\): every cross-section moves in proportion to its distance from the ceiling, the lower end by \(\Delta L = 6{,}496\) mm. In the middle is a field with the same displacement of the lower end, \(u = \Delta L\,x/L + c\,x\,(L - x)\) with \(c = 3{,}2 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), which has a displacement \(0{,}8\) mm larger at the middle of the bar. With it the upper half of the bar is stretched more and the lower half less. The largest strain is at the ceiling, \(9{,}7 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the stress there is \(190\) MPa, below the yield stress \(220\) MPa, so the strain is small and the material linear elastic. At the top is a field that stretches the bar only to \(\Delta L/2\). All three fields are zero at the ceiling, so they are kinematically admissible. The arrows assign one number on the axis \(\Pi\) to each field: \(-32{,}48\) J to the true one, \(-29{,}85\) J to the blue one and \(-24{,}36\) J to the grey one. The true and the blue field have the same displacement of the lower end, so the potential energy of the load is the same for both, \(-F\,\Delta L\). The difference \(2{,}63\) J between their values is therefore the difference of their strain energies, computed with the density \(w = \tfrac12\,E\,u'(x)^2\) in every cross-section. So the value of \(\Pi\) depends not only on the displacement of the end but on the whole field. The true field has the smallest value, and the theorem in the next section says that this holds for every body.

4.6.4 The principle of minimum total potential energy

For the bar with a load the difference between the energy of a state and that of equilibrium was the strain energy of the difference, \(\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2\). For a body we will show the same. First we need a rule for how the strain energy density behaves for a sum of two strains. For the bar it was the expanded square \((e - \Delta L)^2\), and for the uniaxial strain in figure 4.269 it is a triangle, a rectangle and another triangle. For a body \(w\) is a sum of products of strain components, and we get the rule by expanding the products in the same way. We write the strain as the Voigt column of six components, as in section 3.6,

\[\{\varepsilon\} = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}},\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}) ,\]

where \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are the engineering shear strains, and \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\ix{p}}\) is the entry of the column in place \(\ix{p}\), which runs from \(1\) to \(6\). We stack the stresses into the column \(\{\sigma\} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}})\) without factors of two. For a symmetric stress with components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and another symmetric strain with components \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), whose column \(\{\eta\}\) we stack in the same way as \(\{\varepsilon\}\),

\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ &\quad + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{yz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \end{aligned} \tag{4.57}\]

because in the double sum of nine terms every shear pair appears twice, for example \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{yx}} = 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{xy}}\), while in the column the factor two hides in the engineering shear strain.

Before we write the rule for six components, let us look at it for one, where it can be seen (figure 4.269, left). We pull a steel bar with modulus of elasticity \(E = 200\) GPa along its axis. On the axes the strain \(\varepsilon\) along the axis of the bar runs horizontally and the stress \(\sigma\) in the same direction vertically, and the line \(\sigma = E\,\varepsilon\) is Hooke's law. In a uniaxial state the strain energy density is the area under this line (section 3.6). We first stretch the bar to the strain \(5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), where the stress is \(100\) MPa. The grey triangle under the line is the energy density of this strain,

\[w(\varepsilon) = \tfrac12 \cdot 100\ \text{MPa} \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-4} = 25\ \text{kJ/m}^3 .\]

Then we increase the strain by \(\eta = 3 \cdot 10^{-4}\), to \(8 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The area under the line grows by two shapes. The orange rectangle has for its height the stress that was already in the bar and for its width the added strain, so its area is \(\sigma\,\eta = 100\ \text{MPa} \cdot 3 \cdot 10^{-4} = 30\ \text{kJ/m}^3\). This is the work of the stress already present on the added strain. The blue triangle above it has the height \(E\,\eta = 60\) MPa, by which the stress grows during the addition, and the area \(\tfrac12 \cdot 60\ \text{MPa} \cdot 3 \cdot 10^{-4} = 9\ \text{kJ/m}^3\). This is \(w(\eta)\), the energy density the added strain would have alone, since the blue triangle equals the triangle under the line from the origin to \(3 \cdot 10^{-4}\). Together,

\[w(\varepsilon + \eta) = 25 + 30 + 9 = 64\ \text{kJ/m}^3 ,\]

which is indeed the area of the whole triangle of height \(160\) MPa, \(\tfrac12 \cdot 160\ \text{MPa} \cdot 8 \cdot 10^{-4}\). So the energy of a sum is not the sum of the energies, \(25 + 9 = 34\), but is larger by the rectangle. The lemma says that the same cut into a triangle, a rectangle and a triangle holds for all six components at once.

Lemma 4.90 Energy density of a sum of strains (gostota energije vsote deformacij)

Let the material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic and linear elastic, with entries \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) of the material stiffness matrix, and let \(\{\varepsilon\}\) and \(\{\eta\}\) be columns of six strain components that need not be small strains. For every such column \(\{\zeta\}\) let \(w(\{\zeta\}) = \tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}}\sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\zeta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\zeta\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), and let the stress that belongs to it be the column with the entries \(\sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\zeta\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). For a small strain these are the strain energy density (theorem 3.62, item 2) and the stress given by the material law. For the bar of figure 4.269, \(w(\{\varepsilon\})\) is the grey triangle and the stress is the height of the line. Then

\[w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = w(\{\varepsilon\}) + \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\eta\}) , \tag{4.58}\]

where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the stress components that belong to the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the components of the strain \(\{\eta\}\).

Proof

We have to show that the expanded energy density of the sum falls into three parts, for the bar the grey triangle, the orange rectangle and the blue triangle. We use the formula for the energy density and the symmetry of the stiffness matrix.

  1. By the definition of the polynomial \(w\) in the hypothesis of the lemma, the energy density of the sum, for the bar the whole triangle up to the sum of the strains,
    \[w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\big(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} + \{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\big)\big(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}}\big) ,\]
    where \(\ix{p}\) and \(\ix{q}\) run from \(1\) to \(6\).
  2. We expand every term as the product of two brackets and get four double sums, for the bar a triangle, two parts of the rectangle and a triangle:
    \[\frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}} .\]
  3. By the same definition the first sum is \(w(\{\varepsilon\})\) and the last one \(w(\{\eta\})\). For the bar of figure 4.269 these are the grey and the blue triangle.
  4. In the third sum we take out \(\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and get \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). The inner sum is the entry \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the stress that belongs to the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\), so the third sum is \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). For the bar this is half of the orange rectangle, \(\tfrac12\,\sigma\,\eta\).
  5. In the second sum we rename the indices, \(\ix{p}\) to \(\ix{q}\) and \(\ix{q}\) to \(\ix{p}\). The sum runs over all pairs, so it does not change, and it equals \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{q}} \sum_{\ix{p}} C_{\mathrm{qp}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). By item 1 of the theorem on the symmetry of the elastic constants \(C_{\mathrm{qp}} = C_{\mathrm{pq}}\), so this is the third sum from step 4, \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), the other half of the rectangle.
  6. The second and the third sum together give \(\sum_{\ix{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), the whole rectangle, which by equation (4.57) equals \(\sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Together with step 3 this is (4.58).

Source: The squares are expanded in the proof of EP (4.3.19) (p. 183), where this is written for an isotropic material. The lemma as a separate statement and the step-by-step proof are not from the sources.

The lemma is the expansion of the square \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) for a function of six variables: \(a^2\) and \(b^2\) are the triangles, \(2ab\) is the rectangle. It does not ask for small strains, because it only expands a polynomial. We shall need this, since the difference of two small strains need not be small (figure 4.269, right, where the numbers on the number line of one strain component are written as multiples of \(10^{-4}\)): the components \(-0{,}0009\) and \(0{,}0009\) lie in the band between \(-0{,}001\) and \(0{,}001\), in which we count strains as small, but their difference \(0{,}0018\) lies outside it. The middle term is expressed here with the stress and has a physical meaning: the energy density of a sum is the sum of the densities, corrected by the work of the stress of the first strain on the second strain. The symmetry of the stiffness matrix is needed in step 5. Without it the second and the third sum would differ, and we could not write the mixed term with the stress. The symmetry is not an extra demand on the material: every ideally elastic and linearly elastic material has it (theorem 3.62, item 1), that is, a material that gives back all the work put in when it is unloaded. For an isotropic material we check the lemma directly. Its energy density is \(w = \tfrac12\,\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \mu \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\) (section 3.6), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the volumetric strain. Expanding the squares gives the mixed term \(\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\eta_{\mathrm{v}} = \eta_{\mathrm{xx}} + \eta_{\mathrm{yy}} + \eta_{\mathrm{zz}}\). Hooke's law (3.28) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for equal indices and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for different ones, so \(\sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the same.

Now we can state the main theorem of the section. Figure 4.270 shows the two fields the theorem speaks about: the true displacement field and any other field that respects the supports. On the left is the body, fixed to the wall, with the face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) where the displacements are prescribed. On the rest of the surface, \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the prescribed traction \(\bar{\vek t}\) presses on the right half of the top face, the body force \(\vek b\) acts in the material, and the outward normal \(\vek n\) is drawn on the right face. On the right are the body before loading (blackwhite), the true field \(\vek u\) (orange) and another admissible field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) (blue dashed). Both fields leave the left face at the wall. What the difference of the fields is shows at the lower right corner \(Q\), drawn four times magnified at the bottom right. The true field moves it by the orange arrow \(\vek u\), the other field by the blue dashed arrow \(\tilde{\vek u}\). The thick blue arrow \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) leads from the true position of the corner to the other one, so that \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek v\). Every point of the body has such an arrow. At the bottom left is the body as it would be if it were moved from the shape before loading (grey dashed) by the difference field \(\vek v\) alone (blue). At the wall, on the face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the difference is zero, because both fields prescribe the same displacement there. The theorem will say that the strain energy of this blue shape is exactly the amount by which the total potential energy of the other field exceeds that of the true one. The point \(P\), the circle of radius \(\delta\) around it and the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) with edge \(d\) will be needed in the second part of the proof.

Theorem 4.91 Principle of minimum total potential energy (načelo najmanjše celotne potencialne energije)

Let the body be as in theorem 4.82 on the principle of virtual displacements, made of a homogeneous (definition 3.11), ideal elastic and linear elastic material whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero. Let the loads \(\vek b\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\) be independent of the deformation. Let \(\vek u\) be a kinematically admissible displacement field with small strains whose stresses satisfy assumptions 1 to 4 of theorem 4.82: they are continuously differentiable, symmetric, satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.38) in the interior, and \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Then for every kinematically admissible displacement field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) with small strains:

  1. the difference of the total potential energies is the strain energy of the difference of the fields,
    \[\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) - \Pi(\vek u) = U(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u) \ge 0 , \tag{4.59}\]
  2. the equality \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u)\) holds only if the small strain tensor of the difference field \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is zero at every point of the body.

The strain of the field \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) need not be small, just as the difference of two components in the band of small strains can lie outside it, so we compute \(U(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u)\) with the density \(w\) as the polynomial from lemma 4.90.

Proof

We have to show that the difference of the energies falls into an expression from the principle of virtual displacements, which is zero, and the strain energy of the difference of the fields, which is not negative. We follow the computation for the bar with a load.

1. Difference of the energies.

  1. Let \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\), in figure 4.270 the thick blue arrow at the corner \(Q\) and the blue shape at the bottom left. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) the two fields have the same prescribed displacement, so \(\vek v\) is zero there. The difference of two kinematically admissible fields is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.88 and the paragraph after it).
  2. We denote the components of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek v\) by \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial v_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\), where \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). The partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.82, applied to one variable with the other two fixed), so the field \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek v\) has at every point the strain with components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the strain components of the field \(\vek u\).
  3. By lemma 4.90 on the energy density of a sum of strains, at every point \(w(\{\varepsilon\} + \{\eta\}) = w(\{\varepsilon\}) + \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}} + w(\{\eta\})\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the stresses of the field \(\vek u\). At every point of the body this is the cut of figure 4.269: the triangle of the true field, the rectangle of the stress of the true field on the strain of the difference, and the triangle of the difference.
  4. We integrate over the body and use the linearity of the integral over a body (section 4.2):
    \[U(\tilde{\vek u}) = U(\vek u) + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V + U(\vek v) .\]
  5. The loads \(\bar{\vek t}\) and \(\vek b\) are the same for both fields. The scalar product is distributive (lemma 2.12), so \(\vek b\cdot\tilde{\vek u} = \vek b\cdot\vek u + \vek b\cdot\vek v\) and \(\bar{\vek t}\cdot\tilde{\vek u} = \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u + \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek v\). By the linearity of the integral the integrals of the potential energy of the loads split in the same way.
  6. We insert steps 4 and 5 into equation (4.56), which defines the total potential energy, and arrange the terms. The square bracket is the work of the stresses on the difference strain minus the work of the loads on the difference of the displacements:
    \[\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u) + \Big[ \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}} \sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}A \Big] + U(\vek v) .\]
  7. The stresses of the field \(\vek u\) satisfy the assumptions of the principle of virtual displacements, and by step 1 \(\vek v\) is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement with virtual strain \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By theorem 4.82 the expression in square brackets is therefore zero: the work of the stress of the true field on the strain of the difference, the sum of all the rectangles over the body, equals the work of the loads \(\bar{\vek t}\) and \(\vek b\) on the displacements \(\vek v\). Hence \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) - \Pi(\vek u) = U(\vek v)\).
  8. The polynomial \(w\) is zero at the zero column. In figure 4.271 on the left the axes carry the number \(\alpha\) by which we multiply the column \(\{\eta\}\) horizontally and \(w(\alpha\{\eta\})\) vertically, and \(w\) of the zero column is the origin. At every column \(\{\eta\} \ne 0\) it is positive, also when \(\{\eta\}\) is not a small strain, like the strain of a bar stretched by \(18 \cdot 10^{-4}\). Indeed, choose a number \(\alpha > 0\) so small that \(\alpha\{\eta\}\) is a small strain, in the figure in the grey band. Every term of the polynomial \(w\) has two strain factors, so \(w(\alpha\{\eta\}) = \alpha^2\,w(\{\eta\})\), a parabola through the origin. At the small strain \(\alpha\{\eta\} \ne 0\) the polynomial \(w\) is the strain energy density, which is positive by assumption (the part of the parabola in the band), so \(w(\{\eta\}) = w(\alpha\{\eta\})/\alpha^2 > 0\) (the point at \(\alpha = 1\)). For the bar, at \(\alpha = 0{,}5\) the strain \(9 \cdot 10^{-4}\) is still in the band and \(w = 81\ \text{kJ/m}^3\), so \(w(\{\eta\}) = 81\ \text{kJ/m}^3/0{,}5^2 = 324\ \text{kJ/m}^3\). Hence \(w(\{\eta\}) \ge 0\) at every point. The integral over a box is an iterated integral (definition 4.8), and each of the three iterated integrals of a nonnegative function is nonnegative (lemma 3.54, item 4). The integral over the body is the sum of the integrals over its boxes (section 4.2), so \(U(\vek v) \ge 0\). This is the strain energy of the blue shape, a sum of blue triangles only, which lie above the axis.

2. Equality.

  1. Let \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u)\). By item 1, \(U(\vek v) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), where \(g = w(\{\eta\})\) at every point of the body, for the bar the blue triangle.
  2. The function \(g\) is continuous at every point of the body. The field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable, so the components \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuous functions of the point, and \(g\) is a sum of products of two of them with constant numbers \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\), which are the same at every point because the material is homogeneous, and it is continuous by corollary 1.70 on the continuity of sums, products and polynomials in space. By step 8 of item 1, \(g \ge 0\), the blue triangle lies above the axis. In figure 4.272, where \(g\) is drawn along a line through the body, the curve never goes below the axis.
  3. Suppose that \(g(P) > 0\) at some interior point \(P\) of the body, on the line the peak of the curve. By the definition of continuity 1.68 with the allowed error \(g(P)/2\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(g > g(P)/2\) at all points of the body closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\) (the dashed circle). On the line this is the band of width \(2\delta\) in which the curve lies above the dashed height \(g(P)/2\).
  4. Since \(P\) is an interior point, a small cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) with centre \(P\) and edge \(d > 0\) lies in the body around it, with its corners closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\). On it \(g > g(P)/2\), and on the line the edge \(d\) lies in the band.
  5. To the grid that cuts the body into cells we add the six planes in which the faces of the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) lie. The integral over the body does not change, because it does not depend on the grid (section 4.2), and the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) is now a union of cells. The integral over the body is the sum of the integrals over the cells. By step 8 of item 1, applied to each cell, none of them is negative (the grey area), so the sum is not smaller than the sum of the integrals over the cells of the cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\), that is than the integral over \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\).
  6. On \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) we have \(g > g(P)/2\), so by monotonicity and the rule for a constant function, applied to the three iterated integrals (lemma 3.54, items 3 and 4), the integral over \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) is not smaller than \(\tfrac12\,g(P)\,d^3\). On the line this is the orange rectangle of height \(g(P)/2\) and width \(d\) under the curve. So the cube alone already contributes a positive energy, which the rest of the body cannot cancel, because it contributes nothing negative anywhere: \(U(\vek v) \ge \tfrac12\,g(P)\,d^3 > 0\), which contradicts step 1. So \(g = 0\) at every interior point.
  7. Every point on the surface of the body is the limit of a sequence of interior points, as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.82, and \(g\) is continuous, so by lemma 1.69 on continuity through sequences of points \(g = 0\) on the surface too.
  8. By step 8 of item 1 the polynomial \(w\) is positive at every column that is not zero. Since \(g = w(\{\eta\}) = 0\) at every point, \(\{\eta\}\) is the zero strain at every point, also in the difference field.

Source: EP §4.3.1, (4.3.6), (4.3.19)-(4.3.20) (pp. 179-183), CM (7.6.14) (PDF p. 346), SADD §6.6 (PDF p. 139), which states the principle and leaves the proof to other books. EP proves the minimum only for an isotropic material, by expanding the squares in the Navier equations. The proof with lemma 4.90 and item 2 are not from the sources. For a body cut into pieces between graphs, such as the round bar, item 1 holds, because the principle of virtual displacements holds for it (end of section 4.5.4) and so does the monotonicity of the integral (lemma 4.22). Item 2 holds for it and for other bodies with a curved surface as far as the rules of step 5 hold for the integral over such a body, which LEBL2 §10.3-10.5 (PDF pp. 108-127) gives.

What does the theorem say? The true displacement field has the smallest total potential energy among all fields that respect the supports.
