Every other field has a larger or equal one, and the difference is exactly the strain energy the body would have if it were deformed by the difference of the two fields. For a body this is the same as the term \(\tfrac12\,k\,(e - \Delta L)^2\) in equation (4.54) was for the bar with a load. The proof has shown where this comes from. The mixed term of the expanded energy, the work of the stress of the true field on the strain of the difference (the rectangle), cancels against the potential energy of the loads on the difference, because the true field is in equilibrium and the difference is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. Only the energy of the difference remains (the blue triangle), which is not negative because the material is stable.

Item 2 tells when another field has the same energy as the true one. The difference must be free of strain. For a body held by its supports so that it can neither move nor turn as a rigid body, as the weld over the whole face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) holds it, such a difference can only be zero. A field without strain is a small rigid displacement by theorem 1.140, and this one is zero because it is zero on the whole face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). The true field is the only one with this energy. We will use the same fact in section 4.8.

Where does the theorem stop holding? Each of the assumptions was needed. Without loads independent of the deformation, the potential energy of the loads of the form \(-\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A\) does not exist. The assumption means that the force \(\bar{\vek t}\) stays vertical and equally large even when the face under it tilts, like the weight of a load placed on the body. In figure 4.273 on the left the face tilts into the orange position, while the weight of the load stays vertical and equally long. Step 5 of the proof used this when it multiplied the same \(\bar{\vek t}\) and the same \(\vek b\) by the displacements of both fields. The pressure of a gas does not satisfy this assumption. In the middle of the figure the pressure \(p\) stays perpendicular to the tilted face, so its direction turns by the same angle \(\theta\) by which the face tilted. At \(\theta = 0{,}01\) rad the pressure gets the horizontal component \(p\,\sin\theta \approx 0{,}01\,p\). This is how much it differs from a load that would stay vertical, and the difference grows in proportion to the angle of rotation.

Without linearity and the symmetry of the stiffness matrix, lemma 4.90 does not hold. Homogeneity was used in step 2 of item 2 of the proof: since the \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) are the same numbers at every point, \(g\) is continuous. For a piece glued from two materials the \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) jump at the joint, and \(g\) with them, so this proof does not suffice for it. We would have to repeat it on each part separately and use at the joint that the forces with which the parts act on each other are equal and opposite.

We need small strains of the true and the other field because the stress by the material law and the strain energy density are given only for strains in the band of small strains (theorem 3.62).

A positive energy density is a measured fact for metals: a bar has to be pulled to become longer, so \(E > 0\) and the triangles lie above the axis, for steel with \(25\ \text{kJ/m}^3\) already at the strain \(5 \cdot 10^{-4}\). For all strains, however, \(E > 0\) alone is not enough. For an isotropic material theorem 3.64 also requires \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\), as for steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\). Figure 4.271 on the right shows a material with \(E = 200\) GPa and \(\nu = 1\), whose bulk modulus \(K\) is negative, \(K/E = -1/3\). A bar of it has in tension up to \(5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) the same energy density as a steel one, \(25\ \text{kJ/m}^3\). But a cube that we stretch equally by \(5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) in all three directions has the density \(-75\ \text{kJ/m}^3\). For it all deviatoric strains \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are zero and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 15 \cdot 10^{-4}\), so by equation (3.72) \(w = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot (-\tfrac{200}{3}\ \text{GPa}) \cdot (15 \cdot 10^{-4})^2\). Such a material would stretch by itself, so it does not exist. Without a positive energy density, step 8 fails, and the true field may only be a point where the derivative of the energy in every direction is zero, not the smallest value, as we will see in subsection 4.6.6.

For large displacements, finally, a compressed bar may bend sideways (figure 4.273, right), and the straight shape is no longer the shape with the smallest energy. EP shows that for a bar in which the term due to large rotations is kept, the minimum cannot be guaranteed when the axial force is compressive (EP Example 4.3.1, pp. 184-187). We do not treat buckling in this chapter.

4.6.5 The bracket of two bars

Let us test the principle on the bracket from section 4.1 (figure 4.274, left). We know its setting, so we only show in the figure what we will need. The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, and the origin is at the joint \(C = (0, 0, 0)\). The horizontal bar \(AC\) has length \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m, and its end \(A = (-4, 0, 0)\) m is pinned to the wall. The inclined bar \(BC\) has length \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m, and its end \(B = (-4, 3, 0)\) m is also pinned to the wall. At the joint \(C\) a load acts with the force \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\), \(F = 10\) kN, which is independent of the deformation. For both bars \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}} = E A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N. In section 4.1 we got from the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac53 F = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -\tfrac43 F = -13{,}33\) kN and the energy \(U = 53{,}57\) J. There we estimated the component \(v\) of the displacement of the joint from the equality of work and energy as \(v = -10{,}71\) mm.

The state of the bracket is described by two numbers. The pins \(A\) and \(B\) do not move and the bars are straight, so everything is fixed by the displacement of the joint \(C\). As in sections 4.1 and 4.4 we write it as \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\). The third component is zero because the pins let the bars turn only in the \(xy\) plane. If the bars could turn about \(A\) and \(B\) in every direction, a displacement of the joint along \(z\) would not lengthen the bars to first order, since it is perpendicular to both, the energy would not change, and the true displacement would not be unique. The number \(u\) is the horizontal displacement, positive to the right, the number \(v\) the vertical displacement, positive upward. In section 4.4 we got the displacement of the joint from the elongations of the bars, and these from the axial forces, which we knew from the equilibrium of the pin. Now let us find it with energy, without knowing the axial forces in advance. Every pair of numbers \(u\), \(v\) is an admissible state, since it respects both pins. For every such state let us compute the total potential energy.

  1. Let us look at the joint from close up (figure 4.275, left). The joint \(C\) with the ends of the bars before loading, which we draw grey and dashed, moves by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) to the position \(C_1\), and we draw the bars after loading orange. For a small displacement of the joint a bar lengthens by the projection of the displacement of the joint onto the direction of the bar, as we saw for virtual displacements in section 4.4. With the unit vectors from the pin toward the joint, \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\), the elongations are
    \[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = u , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v .\]
    The figure shows the true displacement, which we have yet to compute. The bar \(AC\) shortens by the horizontal part of the displacement, 2,721 mm. We extend the direction of the bar \(BC\) beyond the joint and drop a perpendicular onto it from \(C_1\). The bar \(BC\) lengthens by the segment from \(C\) to the foot of the perpendicular, 4,252 mm. The vertical part of the displacement is 10,71 mm.

Why may we take the projection? The exact new length of a bar is the distance from the pin to \(C_1\). The projection leaves out the part of the displacement that is perpendicular to the bar and almost only turns it. Let us see how much this part lengthens the bar all the same (figure 4.276). We draw the bar \(BC\) horizontally, with the pin at \(B\) and the end at \(C\), of length \(L\). We move the end perpendicular to the bar by \(p\). The bar in its new position is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the legs \(L\) and \(p\), so by the Pythagorean theorem its length is \(\sqrt{L^2 + p^2}\). The arc with centre \(B\) and radius \(L\) marks off the length \(L\) on it, and what remains to the end is the extra length

\[\sqrt{L^2 + p^2} - L = \frac{p^2}{\sqrt{L^2 + p^2} + L} \approx \frac{p^2}{2L} .\]

We get the first equality by multiplying and dividing the left side by \(\sqrt{L^2 + p^2} + L\), since \((\sqrt{L^2 + p^2} - L)(\sqrt{L^2 + p^2} + L) = L^2 + p^2 - L^2 = p^2\). The denominator is almost \(2L\), because \(p\) is much smaller than \(L\). For the bar \(BC\) the perpendicular part is 10,20 mm, 490 times less than \(L = 5000\) mm, so the denominator differs from \(2L\) by only about one millionth, and what is left out is \(10{,}20^2/(2 \cdot 5000)\ \text{mm} = 0{,}010\) mm of 4,252 mm, for the bar \(AC\) it is \(10{,}71^2/(2 \cdot 4000)\ \text{mm} = 0{,}014\) mm of 2,721 mm, so 0,2 % and 0,5 % of the elongation. The assumption holds as long as the displacements are small compared with the lengths of the bars, here 11 mm against 4 m. For displacements comparable with the length of the bars we would have to compute with the exact distance, and the energy would no longer be a polynomial of degree two.

  1. A bar with elongation \(\Delta L\) carries the axial force \(N = EA\,\Delta L/L\) and stores the energy \(N^2 L/(2EA)\) (theorem 4.3). The relation \(N = EA\,\Delta L/L\) holds because the bars are linear elastic: in the true state the bar \(BC\) has the stress 166,7 MPa, 76 % of the yield stress 220 MPa (section 4.1.4). Above the yield stress the force would no longer grow in proportion to the elongation, and the energy would not be a square of the elongation. Inserting the force, the energy is \(EA\,\Delta L^2/(2L)\). The energy of the bracket is the sum of the energies of the two bars:
    \[U(u, v) = \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,u^2 + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\big(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\big)^2 .\]
  2. The load is independent of the deformation, so its potential energy is \(-\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -\big(0 \cdot u + (-F)\,v\big) = F\,v\). A load that goes down has \(v < 0\), and its potential energy is negative, as for the bar with a load.
  3. The total potential energy is the sum. With numbers, \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}/(2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}) = 2{,}45 \cdot 10^6\) N/m and \(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}/(2 L_{\mathrm{BC}}) = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, and expanding the square,
    \[\begin{aligned} \Pi(u, v) &= 3{,}7044 \cdot 10^6\,u^2 - 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\,u\,v \\ &\quad + 0{,}7056 \cdot 10^6\,v^2 + 10^4\,v , \end{aligned} \tag{4.60}\]
    with displacements in metres and energy in joules. The numbers in front of the squares and the product come about like this:
    \[\begin{aligned} 3{,}7044 \cdot 10^6 &= 2{,}45 \cdot 10^6 + 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 0{,}8^2 , \\ 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6 &= 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 2 \cdot 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 , \\ 0{,}7056 \cdot 10^6 &= 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 0{,}6^2 . \end{aligned}\]
    The product has a minus, because the bracket contains \(-0{,}6\,v\), and the number \(10^4\) is the load \(F = 10\,000\) N. The number in front of \(u^2\) is more than five times the number in front of \(v^2\). What this means we will see on the contour lines of figure 4.278 and on the parabolas of figure 4.280.

Theorem 4.91 is about a body, while we described the bracket with the truss model, in which every bar is only an elongation and an axial force. So we repeat the computation of the proof for the bracket, where it is simpler. Let \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) be the true displacement of the joint from section 4.4, at which the bars carry the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}\) from section 4.1, and let \(\vek w = (w_{\mathrm{x}}, w_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) be any vector. The right half of figure 4.275 shows again the bars before loading and in the true state with the joint at the true position \(C_1\). The vector \(\vek w\) moves it to another position \(C_2\). For the figure we chose \(\vek w = (2{,}721\ \text{mm}, 0, 0)\), for which \(C_2\) is vertically below the position \(C\) before loading. The computation holds for every \(\vek w\).

  1. The elongation of a bar for the displacement \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek w\) is \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w\), by the distributivity of the scalar product, and the same for \(BC\). So the projection of the vector \(\vek w\) onto the direction of the bar is added to the elongation of the true state. In the figure these are \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w = 2{,}721\) mm and, with the perpendicular from \(C_2\) onto the direction of the bar \(BC\), \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w = 0{,}8 \cdot 2{,}721\ \text{mm} = 2{,}177\) mm.
  2. We expand the square of the sum, \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\), where \(a = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the elongation of the bar in the true state and \(b = \vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w\) the projection of the vector \(\vek w\) on the direction of the bar. The energy of the bar \(AC\) is therefore
    \[\frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})^2 + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w) + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w)^2 ,\]
    and the same for \(BC\). The first term is the energy of the bar in the true state.
  3. In the middle term \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}})/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = E A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = N_{\mathrm{AC}}\), the axial force of the true state. The middle term is therefore \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w)\), the axial force times the projection of the vector \(\vek w\).
  4. For the displacement \(\vek w\) the potential energy of the load changes by \(-\vek F\cdot\vek w\). All together:
    \[\begin{aligned} \Pi(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek w) - \Pi(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}) &= \big[ N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w - \vek F\cdot\vek w \big] \\ &\quad + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w)^2 + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{2 L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w)^2 . \end{aligned}\]
  5. The expression in square brackets is \((N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} - \vek F)\cdot\vek w\). The equilibrium of the pin \(C\) from section 4.1, \(\vek F - N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek 0\), says that the vector in the bracket is the zero vector. This is also the principle of virtual displacements for the truss from section 4.4 with the virtual displacement \(\vek w\). Let us check with numbers: \(-13\,333\ \text{N} \cdot (1, 0, 0) + \tfrac15 \cdot 16\,667\ \text{N} \cdot (4, -3, 0) = (0, -10\,000, 0)\ \text{N} = \vek F\).
  6. Two squares remain, the squares of the projections of the vector \(\vek w\) onto the bar \(AC\) and onto the bar \(BC\), which are not negative. Both are zero only if \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\cdot\vek w = w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\cdot\vek w = 0{,}8\,w_{\mathrm{x}} - 0{,}6\,w_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), so \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). Every other displacement of the joint therefore has a larger energy than the true one, and there is only one true displacement.

Now let us find the true displacement. Where \(\Pi\) has its smallest value, the function of one variable that we get by holding one component fixed, along the horizontal or vertical line has its smallest value too. Its derivative is zero there (lemma 1.83), and this derivative is a partial derivative of \(\Pi\) (definition 1.26). From steps 2 and 3 of the energy computation, with \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4{,}9 \cdot 10^6\) N/m and \(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}/L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 3{,}92 \cdot 10^6\) N/m, we get

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial u} &= \frac{E A_{\mathrm{AC}}}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,u + \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\big(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\big) \cdot 0{,}8 = 0 , \\ \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial v} &= \frac{E A_{\mathrm{BC}}}{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\big(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\big) \cdot (-0{,}6) + F = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

What do the two equations say? The expression \(E A_{\mathrm{AC}}\,u/L_{\mathrm{AC}}\) is the axial force of the bar \(AC\), and the expression \(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}\,(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v)/L_{\mathrm{BC}}\) the axial force of the bar \(BC\). So the equations are \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} + 0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) and \(-0{,}6\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} + F = 0\), the \(x\) and \(y\) components of the equilibrium of the pin \(C\) with the sign changed. The derivatives of the total potential energy are exactly the equilibrium equations of the joint. The second gives \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F/0{,}6 = 16{,}67\) kN, the first \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -0{,}8\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -13{,}33\) kN, as in section 4.1. The elongations are \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = N_{\mathrm{BC}} L_{\mathrm{BC}}/(E A_{\mathrm{BC}}) = 4{,}252\) mm and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = -2{,}721\) mm. From \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u\) and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\) it follows that

\[u = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} , \qquad v = \frac{0{,}8\,u - \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{0{,}6} = \frac{-2{,}177 - 4{,}252}{0{,}6}\ \text{mm} = -10{,}71\ \text{mm} .\]

We checked with SymPy that the smallest value of the function (4.60) lies at \(u = -2/735\) m and \(v = -3/280\) m, which is the same, and that \(\Pi = -53{,}57\) J there.

The joint moves 2,721 mm to the left and 10,71 mm down (figure 4.274, right). In the right half of the figure the bracket before loading is blackwhite, after it orange, the joint \(C\) goes to the position \(C_1\), and the pins \(A\) and \(B\) on the wall do not move. To the left because the compressed bar \(AC\) shortens and the joint stays at its end.

Down, however, almost four times as much. Why? The bar \(BC\) has to lengthen by 4,252 mm, because it carries the axial force 16,67 kN. We split the displacement of the joint into two parts and project each onto the direction of the bar \(BC\) (figure 4.277). The bar \(BC\) ends at the joint \(C\), and we extend its direction beyond the joint. The vertical part of the displacement, 10,71 mm, does not lengthen the bar \(AC\) to first order, since it is perpendicular to it. The perpendicular from its end onto the direction of the bar \(BC\) shows that it lengthens the bar \(BC\) by only \(0{,}6 \cdot 10{,}71\ \text{mm} = 6{,}43\) mm. The number \(0{,}6\) is the vertical component of the unit vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\): the bar drops 3 m over its 5 m length. The horizontal part, 2,721 mm to the left, which brings the joint to the position \(C_1\), shortens the bar \(BC\) by \(0{,}8 \cdot 2{,}721\ \text{mm} = 2{,}177\) mm, since the bar moves 4 m to the right over its 5 m length. The elongation 4,252 mm remains. So the vertical part has to give the elongation and make up for these 2,177 mm as well, while every millimetre of vertical displacement brings only 0,6 mm of elongation. Therefore the vertical part is \((4{,}252 + 2{,}177)/0{,}6\ \text{mm} = 10{,}71\) mm, almost four times 2,721 mm. The bracket is therefore much more flexible vertically than horizontally. This shows in equation (4.60) too, where the number in front of \(v^2\) is more than five times smaller than the number in front of \(u^2\).

Let us also confirm the observation from section 4.1. There we got the component \(v\) of the displacement of the joint from the equality of the work of the load and the energy as \(v = -2U/F\) and promised a proof. For the bracket Clapeyron's theorem reads \(2U = \vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), where \(\vek F\) is the load and \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) the displacement of the joint. We prove it like theorem 4.86, except that in the principle of virtual displacements for the truss from section 4.4 we take the true displacement of the joint instead of a virtual one. The left side of the principle is then \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}\), and each term is twice the energy of the bar, \(N\,\Delta L = 2 \cdot \tfrac12\,N\,\Delta L\) (theorem 4.3). The right side is \(\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). With numbers the left side is \((-13\,333\ \text{N})(-2{,}721\ \text{mm}) + 16\,667\ \text{N} \cdot 4{,}252\ \text{mm} = 36{,}28\ \text{J} + 70{,}86\ \text{J} = 107{,}14\) J, and the right side \((-10\,000\ \text{N})(-10{,}71\ \text{mm}) = 107{,}14\) J. Since \(\vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -F\,v\), we get \(v = -2U/F = -10{,}71\) mm, as estimated. The smallest value of the energy is \(\Pi = U - \vek F\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = U - 2U = -U = -53{,}57\) J, as for the bar with a load, where it was \(-\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\).

Figure 4.278 shows the function (4.60) with contour lines. A contour line (plastnica) is a line along which the function has a constant value, as a contour line on a map connects points of the same height above sea level. In the figure the axis \(u\) and the axis \(v\) show the horizontal and the vertical displacement of the joint \(C\) in millimetres. The contour lines are ellipses with a common centre at the lowest point. They are ellipses because \(\Pi\) is a polynomial of degree two in two variables with a smallest value, and the difference from the smallest value is, by steps 4 and 5 of the repeated proof above, a sum of two squares. The ellipses are elongated. The long axis of the outer ellipse measures \(22{,}2\) mm, the short one \(7{,}3\) mm, \(3{,}02\) times less, and the long axis is tilted \(16°\) from the vertical dashed line, its upper end to the right. This is so because the energy changes slowly along the long axis: to rise by the same amount, we must move from the lowest point three times farther along the long axis than across it. The inner, middle and outer ellipse are the contour lines \(\Pi = -48{,}57\) J, \(-33{,}57\) J and \(0\). The state before loading, \(u = v = 0\), lies on the contour line \(\Pi = 0\). Through the lowest point there also pass the horizontal and vertical dashed lines, along which we will look at the energy.

Let us also test equation (4.59). Take the state in which the joint goes down by the true 10,71 mm but does not move horizontally, \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} + \vek w\) with \(\vek w = (2721, 0, 0)\) µm. The function (4.60) gives \(\Pi = -26{,}14\) J, which is \(27{,}43\) J more than the smallest value. By step 4 of the repeated proof above, the energy of the difference \(\vek w\) is \(2{,}45 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot (2{,}721 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2 + 1{,}96 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot (0{,}8 \cdot 2{,}721 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m})^2 = 18{,}14\ \text{J} + 9{,}29\ \text{J} = 27{,}43\) J, exactly that much. This is just the vector \(\vek w\) of the right half of figure 4.275, and the brackets hold its projections 2,721 mm and 2,177 mm. In the figure of the contour lines this state lies on the horizontal dashed line, 2,721 mm to the right of the lowest point.

4.6.6 The derivative in every direction is zero

For the bracket the partial derivatives of the total potential energy were zero in the true state, the lowest point of the contour lines. This is not special to the bracket. What happens to the energy of a body if we move from some admissible field \(\vek u\) in the direction of an admissible virtual displacement \(\vek v\), by a multiple \(\alpha\,\vek v\)? This time the field \(\vek u\) need not be the true one.

The figure shows the admissible fields as points of a plane. The field \(\vek u\) is a point, the virtual displacement \(\vek v\) an arrow from it. The fields \(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v\) lie on the line through \(\vek u\) in the direction of the arrow, for \(\alpha = 1\) at the tip of the arrow. For a large \(\alpha\) the field is far from \(\vek u\).

  1. The field \(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v\) has the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \alpha\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the strain components of the field \(\vek v\), because the partial derivative of the field \(\alpha\,\vek v\) is \(\alpha\) times the partial derivative of the field \(\vek v\) (lemma 1.82).
  2. In lemma 4.90 we take \(\alpha\,\{\eta\}\) as the second strain, the strain of the field \(\alpha\,\vek v\). The mixed term is \(\alpha \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The last term is \(w(\alpha\,\{\eta\}) = \tfrac12 \sum_{\ix{p}}\sum_{\ix{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,(\alpha\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{p}})(\alpha\,\{\eta\}_{\mathrm{q}}) = \alpha^2\,w(\{\eta\})\), because every term of the energy density has two strain factors. The lemma does not ask \(\alpha\,\{\eta\}\) and \(\{\varepsilon\} + \alpha\,\{\eta\}\) to be small strains, and for a large \(\alpha\) they are not. Then we compute \(w\), and with it \(\Pi(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v)\), with the polynomial from the lemma.
  3. We integrate and add the potential energy of the loads as in the proof of theorem 4.91. The result is a parabola in \(\alpha\):
    \[\Pi(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v) = \Pi(\vek u) + \alpha\,B(\vek v) + \alpha^2\,U(\vek v) , \tag{4.61}\]
    where \(B(\vek v) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\ix{i}}\sum_{\ix{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the internal virtual work of the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) on the virtual displacement \(\vek v\) minus the external virtual work (section 4.5).

Along every direction \(\vek v\) the energy is thus a polynomial of degree two in the number \(\alpha\), a parabola, like the parabolas of the bracket for the horizontal and for the vertical direction in figure 4.280. Its derivative with respect to \(\alpha\) at \(\alpha = 0\) is \(B(\vek v)\), by the rules of differentiation. If \(\vek u\) is the true field, then \(B(\vek v) = 0\) for every admissible virtual displacement by the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.82), and all the parabolas have a horizontal tangent at \(\alpha = 0\). The converse holds too. If \(B(\vek v) = 0\) for every admissible virtual displacement and the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) are continuously differentiable, the virtual work equation holds for every such displacement, and by the converse of the principle of virtual displacements in section 4.5 the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) satisfy the equilibrium equations and the condition \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). An admissible field with continuously differentiable stresses is therefore the true one exactly when the derivative of the total potential energy in every admissible direction is zero at it. Such a point is called a stationary point (stacionarna točka) of the energy, and the condition stationarity (SADD §6.6, PDF p. 139). The expression \(\alpha\,B(\vek v)\), the part of the change of the energy proportional to \(\alpha\), is called the first variation (prva variacija) in EP and written \(\delta\Pi\) (EP (3.5.8), p. 136, and (4.3.2), p. 180). CM uses the same name and symbol for the derivative \(B(\vek v)\) itself, without the factor \(\alpha\) (CM (7.6.1), PDF p. 344).

For the bracket \(U(\vek w)\) is \(3{,}7044\) J for \(\vek w = 1\ \text{mm}\ \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(0{,}7056\) J for \(\vek w = 1\ \text{mm}\ \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), which are the numbers in front of \(u^2\) and \(v^2\) in equation (4.60), converted to millimetres. Along the horizontal line through the lowest point, therefore, \(\Pi = -53{,}57\ \text{J} + 3{,}7044\ \text{J} \cdot \alpha^2\), and along the vertical one \(-53{,}57\ \text{J} + 0{,}7056\ \text{J} \cdot \alpha^2\), with \(\alpha\) in millimetres and \(\Pi\) in joules (figure 4.280). The derivatives along the directions \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) at the lowest point are the partial derivatives from the previous subsection, and both are zero.

Stationarity is weaker than a smallest value (figure 4.281). On both horizontal axes is the number \(\alpha\), on the vertical ones the energy \(\Pi\). Stationarity says only that the tangent at \(\alpha = 0\) along every line is horizontal, not that the energy is larger elsewhere. The right curve has a horizontal tangent at \(\alpha = 0\), but to the left of this point the energy is lower: the derivative is zero, yet this is not the lowest point. For our material \(U(\vek v) \ge 0\). At a stationary point \(B(\vek v) = 0\), so by equation (4.61) along every line \(\Pi(\vek u + \alpha\,\vek v) = \Pi(\vek u) + \alpha^2\,U(\vek v) \ge \Pi(\vek u)\), as for the left parabola, and the stationary point is the lowest point. Stationarity, however, also holds for a nonlinear elastic material, where lemma 4.90 does not hold: EP shows that \(\delta\Pi = 0\) follows from the principle of virtual displacements for every material whose stresses are partial derivatives of an energy density (EP (4.3.2), p. 180). That the stationary point is also the lowest one must then be checked separately. The same holds when the strain is not linear in the displacements. EP shows this on a beam that bends strongly sideways: the stationary point is the lowest one when the axial force stretches the beam, but with a compressive axial force not necessarily, because the integral that would show it is not always positive (EP Example 4.3.1, pp. 184-187).

4.6.7 Castigliano's first theorem

For the bar with a load the strain energy is \(U(e) = \tfrac12\,k\,e^2\) and its derivative \(k\,e\). At the equilibrium elongation this is \(k\,\Delta L = F\), the weight of the load (figure 4.282). In the figure the parabola is the energy \(U\) against the elongation, on the axes \(e\) and \(U\). The point at \(\Delta L\) has the height \(\tfrac12\,F\,\Delta L\), the tangent there meets the axis \(e\) at half of the elongation, and the grey triangle gives from this the slope \(F\). For the bracket the energy \(U(u, v)\) is equation (4.60) without its last term. We differentiate term by term (lemma 1.82): a square gives twice its number, and the mixed term gives \(-1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\) times the other variable for each variable. The partial derivatives are

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial U}{\partial u} &= 7{,}4088 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u - 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v , \\ \frac{\partial U}{\partial v} &= -1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u + 1{,}4112 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v . \end{aligned}\]

At the lowest point of the total potential energy (4.60), at \(u = -2/735\) m \(\approx -2{,}721\) mm and \(v = -3/280\) m \(\approx -10{,}71\) mm, the first derivative is \(0\) and the second \(-10\,000\) N, which we checked with SymPy. These are the \(x\) and \(y\) components of the load \(\vek F = (0, -F, 0)\). The derivative of the strain energy with respect to a displacement is thus the component of the force that acts at the point and in the direction of this displacement.

From history

Alberto Castigliano (1847-1884) was born in Asti and taught for several years, and in 1870 he entered the Turin Polytechnical Institute (TIMO, PDF p. 228). There, as a student, he did outstanding work in the theory of structures. In his thesis of 1873 he stated his theorem with a few applications, and in an extended form the Turin Academy of Sciences published it in 1875. Engineers at first did not see its importance, so in 1879 Castigliano published the work again in French, with a complete proof and many examples (TIMO, PDF p. 228). He began with a truss loaded at the joints. He wrote its strain energy with the displacements of the joints. If the displacements change a little, the energy changes by approximately the work of the external forces on these changes, since the work of the forces is stored in the truss. The error is the gap between the parabola and the tangent, which falls to a quarter when the change is halved. If only one displacement changes by a small \(\delta\), only the corresponding force does work, \(F\,\delta\). So the derivative of the energy with respect to each displacement equals the corresponding force (TIMO, PDF p. 229). The derivative with respect to a force, which Castigliano wrote, we meet in section 4.7.4.

What we saw for the bar with a load in figure 4.282, where the slope of the energy with respect to the elongation equals the weight of the load, we now state as a theorem for an arbitrary structure.

The proof is guided by figure 4.283, which shows what happens when we vary only one displacement.

On the upper axes the curve is the energy \(U(t)\) and the line is the work of the load \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\,t\), whose negative is the potential energy of the load. The tangent to \(U\) at the equilibrium point is parallel to the line. On the lower axes is the difference \(g(t)\) with its lowest point at \(t = \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0\), the horizontal tangent there and the interval around it that we use in the proof.

Theorem 4.92 Castigliano's first theorem (prvi Castiglianov izrek)

Let the state of a structure made of a linear elastic material be fixed by \(n\) numbers \(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}\), components of displacements of chosen points in chosen directions, so that every choice of the numbers gives a state that respects the supports. Let the strain energy be a function \(U(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}})\) that has partial derivatives with respect to all variables. Let only forces independent of the deformation act on the structure, such that the component of the force at the point and in the direction of the displacement \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\) has the value \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the potential energy of the loads is \(-\sum_{\ix{i}} F_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\). If the total potential energy

\[\Pi(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}) = U(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}) - \sum_{\ix{i}} F_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\]

has its smallest value among all choices of the numbers at the equilibrium values of the displacements, then at these values, for every \(\ix{i}\),

\[F_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{\partial U}{\partial \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}} . \tag{4.62}\]
Proof

We have to show that the partial derivative of the total potential energy with respect to each displacement is zero in equilibrium, and compute this derivative.

  1. We denote the equilibrium values by \(\Delta_1^0, \dots, \Delta_{\mathrm{n}}^0\). Choose \(\ix{i}\), and for every number \(t\) let \(g(t)\) be the value of \(\Pi\) when the \(\ix{i}\)-th displacement equals \(t\) and all others equal their equilibrium values.
  2. Every choice of the number \(t\) gives a state that respects the supports, and \(\Pi\) has its smallest value at the equilibrium values among all states, so also among these. The function \(g\) therefore has its smallest value on the interval \([\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0 - h, \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0 + h]\) with any \(h > 0\) (in the figure \(h = 1\)) at the interior point \(t = \Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0\).
  3. The derivative of \(g\) at \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0\) is the partial derivative of \(\Pi\) with respect to \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\) at the equilibrium values, since we vary only one variable and hold the others fixed (definition 1.26, in the same way for \(n\) variables). It exists because \(U\) has it by assumption and the linear term has it by the rules of differentiation.
  4. By lemma 1.83 on the derivative at an interior extremum, \(g'(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0) = 0\).
  5. When only \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\) varies, the term \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a linear function with derivative \(F_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the other terms of the sum \(\sum F_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{j}}\) are constant and have derivative zero (lemma 1.82). Therefore \(g'(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}^0)\) is the difference of the slope of \(U\) and the slope of the line, \(\partial U/\partial\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} - F_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  6. Steps 4 and 5 give that the tangent to \(U\) and the line are parallel, \(\partial U/\partial\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = F_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Source: EP §4.3.2, (4.3.22), (4.3.23) (pp. 188-189), where the theorem is derived from stationarity and holds also for nonlinear elastic materials, and EP Example 4.3.2 (pp. 189-190) for a truss of two bars.

When does \(\Pi\) really have its smallest value at the equilibrium values? For the bar with a load we showed it with equation (4.54), for the bracket with the computation in subsection 4.6.5, and for a body, when the true displacement field is among the fields described by the numbers \(\Delta_{\ix{i}}\), by theorem 4.91. In a truss the state is always fixed by the displacements of the joints, because every bar carries a constant axial force and stretches evenly, and the computation of subsection 4.6.5 repeats with more bars and joints. The proof does not use linear elasticity, only that \(\Pi\) has its smallest value. It is in the theorem because so far we have shown the smallest value only for linear elastic materials. EP derives the theorem from stationarity and therefore states it also for nonlinear elastic materials (EP, p. 188).

What does the theorem say? If we know the strain energy as a function of the displacements, differentiation gives the forces these displacements require. For the bracket the theorem gives two equations that are linear in the displacements:

\[\begin{aligned} 7{,}4088 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u - 1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v &= 0 , \\ -1{,}8816 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot u + 1{,}4112 \cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} \cdot v &= -10\,000\ \text{N} . \end{aligned}\]

Their solution is again \(u = -2{,}721\) mm and \(v = -10{,}71\) mm. The four numbers on the left say how much force is needed for every metre of displacement in each direction. Arranged in a matrix they are the stiffness matrix (togostna matrika) of the bracket (EP Example 4.3.3, p. 191). The matrix is symmetric, because the numbers off the diagonal are the mixed derivatives of the energy, \(\partial^2 U/\partial u\,\partial v\) and \(\partial^2 U/\partial v\,\partial u\), which are equal by theorem 1.131 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives. This is how the finite element method, which we will meet in chapter 7, sets up its equations, with the energy written in terms of the displacements of the joints. We did not compute the bracket with the geometry of intersecting bars but with derivatives of one single function, and this is the route a computer takes too.

4.6.8 Trial fields for the hanging bar

For the bracket the state was described by finitely many numbers. For a body, or for a bar with a load along its length, the displacement is a function, and we often cannot compute the true field. The principle of minimum energy offers a way out. We choose a family of simple fields that respect the supports and depend on a few numbers, write the energy as a function of these numbers and look for the smallest value. We get the best field in the family. Let us try it on the hanging bar, where we know the true field and can compare the approximation with it.

The model is the bar from section 4.4 (figure 4.284, left): a bar of length \(L\), fixed at \(x = 0\), with Young's modulus \(E\) and cross-section area \(A\), loaded by a distributed axial load \(q\), a force per unit length, and by a force \(F\) at the end \(x = L\). The axis \(x\) points along the bar, from the fixing towards the free end. Every cross section moves only along the axis: the cross section that was at \(x\) before loading is after it farther from the fixing by \(u(x)\), and the end of the bar by \(u(L)\). Both displacements are drawn strongly magnified. The axial force is \(N = EA\,u'\), and the energy per unit length is \(\tfrac12\,EA\,u'^2\) (section 4.1). The model is not a special case of a body with \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), since in the bar the cross sections may thin freely. So we state the principle for it separately, with a proof that is the proof of theorem 4.91 carried over to integrals along the length.

Corollary 4.93 Minimum total potential energy of a bar (najmanjša potencialna energija palice)

Let a bar lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and be fixed at \(x = 0\). Let its Young's modulus \(E\) and its cross-section area \(A\) be positive numbers. Let a distributed axial load \(q\), continuous on \([0, L]\), act on it, and at the end \(x = L\) a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), both independent of the deformation. For every function \(u\) that is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, L]\), at the endpoints with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), has a derivative continuous on \([0, L]\), and satisfies \(u(0) = 0\), let

\[\Pi(u) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,u'(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q(x)\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,u(L) . \tag{4.63}\]

Let \(u\) be one of these functions for which the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \((0, L)\), \(N'(x) + q(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in (0, L)\) and \(N(L) = F\). Then for every function \(\tilde u\) that is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, L]\), one-sidedly at the endpoints, with a derivative continuous on \([0, L]\), and with \(\tilde u(0) = 0\)

\[\Pi(\tilde u) - \Pi(u) = \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,\big(\tilde u'(x) - u'(x)\big)^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0 ,\]

with equality only for \(\tilde u = u\).

Proof

We have to show the same splitting as for a body, and then that the integral of a square is zero only for the zero function.

  1. Let \(v = \tilde u - u\) be the difference between the trial field \(\tilde u\) and the true field \(u\), both drawn as functions of \(x\). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82, items 1 and 2), used for one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, \(v\) is differentiable at every point of \([0, L]\) with the derivative \(v' = \tilde u' - u'\), which is continuous as a difference of continuous functions (corollary 1.65), and \(v(0) = 0\), because both fields are zero at the fixing.
  2. We expand the square: \(\tilde u'^2 = (u' + v')^2 = u'^2 + 2\,u'\,v' + v'^2\). This is the square with the side \(\tilde u' = u' + v'\), cut into the square \(u'^2\), two rectangles \(u'\,v'\) and the square \(v'^2\). Therefore \(\tfrac12\,EA\,\tilde u'^2 = \tfrac12\,EA\,u'^2 + N\,v' + \tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\), because \(EA\,u' = N\).
  3. We integrate and use the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 1). In the same way we split \(\int_0^L q\,\tilde u\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,u\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L q\,v\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(F\,\tilde u(L) = F\,u(L) + F\,v(L)\). We get the splitting of the energy of the trial field into the energy of the true field, the expression in square brackets and the strain energy of the difference, the integral of the blue square along the length, all drawn on the energy axis:
    \[\Pi(\tilde u) = \Pi(u) + \Big[ \int_0^L N\,v'\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_0^L q\,v\,\mathrm{d}x - F\,v(L) \Big] + \int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  4. By the principle of virtual displacements for a bar (theorem 4.76) with the virtual displacement \(\delta u = v\), the expression in square brackets is zero: it is the internal virtual work of the axial force less the virtual work of the load \(q\) and of the force \(F\), in the figure two orange columns of equal height. We may do this because \(N\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), since \(u'\) is continuous, and satisfies the equilibrium of the bar, while \(v\) is differentiable at every point of the interval \([0, L]\), one-sidedly at the endpoints, with a continuous derivative and \(v(0) = 0\), so it is a virtual displacement of the bar.
  5. The function \(\tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\), drawn over the same axis \(x\), is not negative, so by the monotonicity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 4) its integral, the area under the graph, is not negative either.
  6. Let the integral of step 5 be zero, and suppose that \(v'(x_0) \ne 0\) at some point \(x_0\) of the interval \([0, L]\). The function \(f = \tfrac12\,EA\,v'^2\) is continuous and \(f(x_0) > 0\). By the definition of continuity 1.59 with the allowed error \(f(x_0)/2\) there is a closed interval \([c, d] \subseteq [0, L]\) with \(c < d\) that contains \(x_0\) and on which \(f > f(x_0)/2\).
  7. By additivity (lemma 3.54, item 2) the integral over \([0, L]\) is the sum of the integrals over \([0, c]\), \([c, d]\) and \([d, L]\), where a piece drops out when \(c = 0\) or \(d = L\). The first and the last are not negative by step 5, and the middle one is not smaller than the area of the rectangle \(\tfrac12\,f(x_0)\,(d - c) > 0\) by item 3 of the same lemma. The integral is therefore positive, which contradicts the assumption. So \(v' = 0\) on \([0, L]\).
  8. By step 1 the function \(v\) is differentiable at every point of \([0, L]\), one-sidedly at the endpoints, so by lemma 1.80, that a differentiable function is continuous, it is continuous on \([0, L]\). So by corollary 1.86 on a function with zero derivative, \(v(x) = v(0) = 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L]\), and \(\tilde u = u\).

Source: EP (3.3.3), (3.3.4) (p. 124) for the total potential energy of bars and beams, EP §4.3.1 (pp. 179-183) for the principle. The step-by-step proof is not from the sources.

The proof showed that every departure from the true field costs energy. The difference of the energies is exactly the area under the function \(f\), and this is positive as soon as the trial field differs from the true one anywhere. At the point where the two fields have the same slope, \(f\) touches the axis, and the area stays positive. The loading entered the proof with one assumption: the load \(q\) and the force \(F\) do not depend on the deformation. For weight this holds, since a piece of the bar weighs the same wherever it moves. It does not hold, for example, for the force of a spring, which grows with the displacement of the end. Then the work of the force is no longer \(F\,u(L)\) with a constant \(F\), the split \(F\,\tilde u(L) = F\,u(L) + F\,v(L)\) of step 3 fails, and with it the equation of the corollary.

The hanging bar (figure 4.284, left) is steel, with length \(L = 10\) m, cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa, so \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N. The top cross section is fixed, \(u(0) = 0\), the axis \(x\) points down, the only load is the weight \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m per unit length, and there is no force at the lower end, \(F = 0\), so the arrow \(F\) drops out here. The true field is \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (section 3.1). Its axial force is \(N = EA \cdot 2a\,(L - x) = \rho g A\,(L - x)\), because \(2aE = \rho g\), and it satisfies \(N' + q = -\rho g A + \rho g A = 0\) and \(N(L) = 0 = F\). By corollary 4.93 the true field therefore has the smallest energy. By Clapeyron's theorem this energy is \(-U = -391{,}03\) µJ, since the work of the weight over the whole displacement is \(2U\).

First trial field: a straight line. Take the fields \(\tilde u(x) = c\,x\) with a free number \(c\), the straight lines through the fixing. All of them respect the fixing, \(\tilde u(0) = 0\). To every number \(c\) belong one line and one energy \(\Pi(c)\), the point of the graph above the number \(c\) in figure 4.286.

  1. The derivative is \(\tilde u' = c\), so the strain is the same everywhere and every metre of the bar stores the same energy \(\tfrac12\,EA\,c^2\), which on the left axes is a horizontal line. The strain energy is the area of the rectangle under it, \(\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,c^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,EA\,c^2 L\) by item 3 of lemma 3.54.
  2. The cross section at depth \(x\) moves by \(c\,x\), so the weight per unit length does the work \(q\,c\,x\) there, which on the right axes is a line rising with the depth. The function \(x^2/2\) has the derivative \(x\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus the potential energy of the weight is \(-\int_0^L q\,c\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\tfrac12\,q\,c\,L^2\), the area of the triangle under the line with the opposite sign.
  3. The total potential energy is \(\Pi(c) = \tfrac12\,EA\,L\,c^2 - \tfrac12\,q\,L^2\,c\), a parabola in \(c\). At \(c = 10^{-6}\) this is the difference of the areas, \(76{,}97 - 300{,}5 = -223{,}5\) µJ, a point of the parabola. At \(c = 0\), when the bar does not move at all, \(\Pi = 0\).
  4. Its derivative is \(EA\,L\,c - \tfrac12\,q\,L^2\). At the lowest point it is zero by lemma 1.83, so \(c = q\,L/(2EA)\). Since \(q = \rho g A\), this is \(c = \rho g L/(2E) = a\,L = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\).

The best straight line is therefore \(\tilde u(x) = a L\,x\) (the lowest point of the parabola in figure 4.286). For it \(\Pi = \tfrac12\,EA\,L\,(aL)^2 - \tfrac12\,\rho g A\,L^2\,aL = \tfrac12\,EA\,a^2 L^3 - EA\,a^2 L^3 = -\tfrac12\,EA\,a^2 L^3\), that is \(-293{,}27\) µJ, where we used \(\rho g = 2aE\) again. Every other line has a higher energy, for example the line with \(c = 10^{-6}\) the energy \(-223{,}5\) µJ. The true field has \(-\tfrac23\,EA\,a^2 L^3 = -391{,}03\) µJ, less, as the principle requires. The difference is \(97{,}76\) µJ.

How good is the approximation? Figure 4.288 shows the displacement \(u\) and the strain \(\varepsilon\) of the bar and two remarkable things. At the lower end the displacement of the line is \(aL \cdot L = aL^2 = 19{,}52\) µm, exactly the true displacement \(u(L) = a\,(2L^2 - L^2) = aL^2\). At the middle, however, the line gives \(9{,}760\) µm instead of \(14{,}64\) µm, a third too little. Why is the displacement of the end exact? The strain of the line is \(aL\) everywhere, while the strain of the true field falls from \(2aL\) at the top to zero at the bottom, and its average is \(aL\), because \(\int_0^L 2a\,(L - x)\,\mathrm{d}x = aL^2\). So the best line has the average strain of the true field. The displacement of the end is the integral of the strain along the length, so it agrees. This is no coincidence. Step 4 requires \(\int_0^L EA\,c\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,x\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the principle of virtual displacements for a bar with the virtual displacement \(\delta u = x\) says that the right side equals \(\int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), where \(N\) is the true axial force. Hence \(EA\,c\,L = \int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), and \(c\) is the average of the true strain \(N/(EA)\). The line is the chord of the parabola from figure 1.328.

The difference of energies, \(97{,}76\) µJ, has a precise meaning. By corollary 4.93 it equals the strain energy of the error, the difference between the trial field and the true field, that is, the area under the function \(f\) of figure 4.284. The error is \(a\,(2Lx - x^2) - aL\,x = a\,(Lx - x^2)\), with the derivative \(a\,(L - 2x)\), and its energy is \(\int_0^L \tfrac12\,EA\,a^2\,(L - 2x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac16\,EA\,a^2 L^3 = 97{,}76\) µJ, which we computed with the function \((2x - L)^3/6\), whose derivative is \((2x - L)^2\). Looking for the smallest energy in a family of fields thus picks the field whose error has the smallest strain energy. The error in energy, \(97{,}76\) µJ out of \(391{,}03\) µJ, is a quarter, the error in the displacement at the middle a third, and the error in the displacement of the end zero. The energy measure is an average over the whole bar, and single points may be better or worse than it.

Second trial field: a parabola. Take the fields \(\tilde u(x) = c_1\,x + c_2\,x^2\) with two free numbers, the parabolas through the fixing. One of them is the blue curve in figure 4.284.

  1. The derivative is \(\tilde u' = c_1 + 2c_2\,x\), its square \(c_1^2 + 4c_1 c_2\,x + 4c_2^2\,x^2\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus with the functions \(x\), \(x^2/2\) and \(x^3/3\) the strain energy is \(\tfrac12\,EA\,\big(c_1^2 L + 2c_1 c_2 L^2 + \tfrac43\,c_2^2 L^3\big)\).
  2. The potential energy of the weight is \(-q\,\big(\tfrac12\,c_1 L^2 + \tfrac13\,c_2 L^3\big)\).
  3. The partial derivatives of the total potential energy with respect to \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are zero at the lowest point, as for the bracket, where both parabolas have a horizontal tangent at the lowest point:
    \[EA\,(c_1 L + c_2 L^2) - \tfrac12\,q\,L^2 = 0 , \qquad EA\,\big(c_1 L^2 + \tfrac43\,c_2 L^3\big) - \tfrac13\,q\,L^3 = 0 .\]
  4. We divide the first equation by \(EA\,L\) and the second by \(EA\,L^2\), and use \(q/(EA) = \rho g/E = 2a\): \(c_1 + c_2 L = aL\) and \(c_1 + \tfrac43\,c_2 L = \tfrac23\,aL\).
  5. We subtract the first from the second: \(\tfrac13\,c_2 L = -\tfrac13\,aL\), so \(c_2 = -a\). The first then gives \(c_1 = aL + aL = 2aL\).

The best parabola is \(2aL\,x - a\,x^2 = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), exactly the true field, and its energy is \(-391{,}03\) µJ. Why exactly? The family contains the true field, since we get it for \(c_1 = 2aL\) and \(c_2 = -a\). By corollary 4.93 the true field has a smaller energy than all other admissible fields, so also than all other parabolas, and the search for the smallest value in the family finds it. We checked with SymPy that the system of step 3 gives exactly these two numbers.

The example shows the idea that we will develop into a systematic computation with trial fields in chapter 6. Every family of trial fields gives an energy that is not smaller than the true one, so every trial computation is an estimate of the true energy from above (CM, PDF p. 343): every point of the parabola in figure 4.286 lies above the line of the true energy. A richer family that contains a poorer one gives an estimate at least as good, since it searches among more fields. The finite element method of chapter 7 cuts the bar into pieces and takes a straight line on each piece, which is a family that we can make as rich as we like by a finer division.

With this we have answered the question from the start of the section. For a body made of an ideal elastic and linear elastic material with loads independent of the deformation, the total potential energy of the true displacement field is the smallest among all kinematically admissible fields. We proved this by splitting the energy of any admissible field into the energy of the true field, the work of the stresses on the difference, which the principle of virtual displacements cancels against the potential energy of the loads, and the strain energy of the difference, which is not negative. Clapeyron's theorem, from the principle of virtual displacements with the true field in place of a virtual one, gave \(2U\) as the work of the full loads, and so confirmed that the work of slow loading is stored completely. For the bracket, the search for the smallest value of a function of two displacements gave the displacement of the joint, 2,721 mm to the left and 10,71 mm down, and the derivatives of the energy gave the equilibrium of the joint and Castigliano's first theorem. For the hanging bar the two trial fields showed how the principle picks the best approximation: the lowest point among the energies of the family. The principle searches among displacement fields that respect the supports and gets the equilibrium as the condition for the smallest value. In the next section we swap the roles: we will search among stresses that are in equilibrium, and the condition will be that the strains fit the displacements and the supports. For this we will need the complementary strain energy density from section 3.6.
